original.text: 亢之為言也，知進而不知退，知存而不知亡，知得而不知喪；其唯聖人乎？知進退存亡而不失其正者，其唯聖人乎！

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-01
original.text: 坤至柔而動也剛，至靜而德方。後得主而有常，含萬物而化光。坤道其順乎！承天而時行。

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-02
original.text: 積善之家，必有餘慶；積不善之家，必有餘殃。臣弒其君，子弒其父，非一朝一夕之故，其所由來者漸矣。由辨之不早辨也。易曰：「履霜，堅冰至。」蓋言順也。

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-03
original.text: 直其正也，方其義也。君子敬以直內，義以方外，敬義立而德不孤。「直方大，不習无不利。」則不疑其所行也。

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-04
original.text: 陰雖有美，含之。以從王事，弗敢成也。地道也，妻道也，臣道也。地道无成，而代有終也。

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-05
original.text: 天地變化，草木蕃；天地閉，賢人隱。易曰：「括囊，无咎，无譽。」蓋言謹也。

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-06
original.text: 君子黃中通理，正位居體，美在其中，而暢於四支，發於事業，美之至也。

original.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-07
original.text: 陰疑於陽必戰，為其嫌於无陽也，故稱龍焉。猶未離其類也，故稱血焉。夫玄黃者，天地之雜也。天玄而地黃。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-01-01
original.text: 天尊地卑，乾坤定矣。卑高以陳，貴賤位矣。動靜有常，剛柔斷矣。方以類聚，物以羣分，吉凶生矣。在天成象，在地成形，變化見矣。是故剛柔相摩，八卦相荡，鼓之以雷霆，潤之以風雨，日月運行，一寒一暑。乾道成男，坤道成女；乾知大始，坤作成物；乾以易知，坤以簡能；易則易知，簡則易從；易知則有親，易從則有功；有親則可久，有功則可大；可久則賢人之德，可大則賢人之業。易簡，而天下之理得矣。天下之理得，而成位乎其中矣。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-02-01
original.text: 聖人設卦觀象，繫辭焉而明吉凶；剛柔相推而生變化。是故吉凶者，失得之象也。悔吝者，憂虞之象也。變化者，進退之象也。剛柔者，晝夜之象也。六爻之動，三極之道也。是故君子所居而安者，易之序也。所樂而玩者，爻之辭也。是故君子居則觀其象而玩其辭，動則觀其變而玩其占；是以自天祐之，吉无不利。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-03-01
original.text: 彖者，言乎象者也。爻者，言乎變者也。吉凶者，言乎其失得也。悔吝者，言乎其小疵也。无咎者，善補過也。是故列貴賤者存乎位，齊小大者存乎卦，辯吉凶者存乎辭，憂悔吝者存乎介，震无咎者存乎悔。是故卦有小大，辭有險易，辭也者，各指其所之。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-04-01
original.text: 易與天地準，故能彌綸天地之道。仰以觀於天文，俯以察於地理，是故知幽明之故。原始反終，故知死生之說。精氣為物，遊魂為變，是故知鬼神之情狀。與天地相似，故不違；知周乎萬物，而道濟天下，故不過；旁行而不流，樂天知命，故不憂；安土敦乎仁，故能愛；範圍天地之化而不過，曲成萬物而不遺，通乎晝夜之道而知，故神无方而易无體。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-05-01
original.text: 一陰一陽之謂道：繼之者善也，成之者性也；仁者見之謂之仁，知者見之謂之知；百姓日用而不知，故君子之道鮮矣。顯諸仁，藏諸用，鼓萬物而不與聖人同憂，盛德大業至矣哉！富有之謂大業，日新之謂盛德，生生之謂易，成象之謂乾，效法之謂坤，極數知來之謂占，通變之謂事，陰陽不測之謂神。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-06-01
original.text: 夫易，廣矣！大矣！以言乎遠則不禦，以言乎邇則靜而正，以言乎天地之間則備矣！夫乾，其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉。夫坤，其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。廣大配天地，變通配四時，陰陽之義配日月，易簡之善配至德。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-07-01
original.text: 子曰：「易其至矣乎！夫易，聖人所以崇德而廣業也，知崇禮卑，崇效天，卑法地。天地設位，而易行乎其中矣。成性存存，道義之門。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-01
original.text: 聖人有以見天下之賾，而擬諸其形容，象其物宜，是故謂之象。聖人有以見天下之動，而觀其會通，以行其典禮，繫辭焉以斷其吉凶，是故謂之爻。言天下之至賾而不可惡也，言天下之至動而不可亂也。擬之而後言，議之而後動，擬議以成其變化。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-02
original.text: 「鳴鶴在陰，其子和之。我有好爵，吾與爾靡之。」子曰：「君子居其室，出其言善，則千里之外應之，況其邇者乎！居其室，出其言不善，則千里之外違之，況其邇者乎！言出乎身加乎民；行發乎邇見乎遠。言行，君子之樞機；樞機之發，榮辱之主也。言行，君子之所以動天地也，可不慎乎！」「同人，先號咷而後笑。」子曰：「君子之道，或出或處，或默或語。二人同心，其利斷金。同心之言，其臭如蘭。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-03
original.text: 「初六，藉用白茅，无咎。」子曰：「苟錯諸地而可矣。藉之用茅，何咎之有！慎之至也。夫茅之為物薄而用可重也，慎斯術也以往，其无所失矣。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-04
original.text: 「勞謙，君子有終，吉。」子曰：「勞而不伐，有功而不德，厚之至也；語以其功下人者也。德言盛，禮言恭；謙也者，致恭以存其位者也。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-05
original.text: 「亢龍有悔。」子曰：「貴而无位，高而无民，賢人在下位而无輔，是以動而有悔也。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-06
original.text: 「不出戶庭，无咎。」子曰：「亂之所生也，則言語以為階。君不密則失臣，臣不密則失身，幾事不密則害成；是以君子慎密而不出也。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-07
original.text: 子曰：「作易者，其知盜乎！易曰：『負且乘，致寇至。』負也者，小人之事也。乘也者，君子之器也。小人而乘君子之器，盜思奪之矣。上慢下暴，盜思伐之矣。慢藏誨盜，冶容誨淫。易曰：『負且乘，致寇至。』盜之招也。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-09-01
original.text: 天一地二，天三地四，天五地六，天七地八，天九地十。天數五，地數五，五位相得而各有合。天數二十有五，地數三十，凡天地之數，五十有五，此所以成變化，而行鬼神也。大衍之數五十，其用四十有九，分而為二以象兩，掛一以象三，揲之以四以象四時，歸奇於扐以象閏，五歲再閏，故再扐而後掛。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-09-02
original.text: 乾之策，二百一十有六，坤之策，百四十有四，凡三百有六十，當期之日。二篇之策，萬有一千五百二十，當萬物之數也。是故四營而成易，十有八變而成卦，八卦而小成；引而伸之，觸類而長之，天下之能事畢矣。顯道神德行，是故可與酬酢，可與祐神矣。子曰：「知變化之道者，其知神之所為乎！」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-01
original.text: 易有聖人之道四焉：以言者尚其辭，以動者尚其變，以制器者尚其象，以卜筮者尚其占。是以君子將有為也，將有行也，問焉而以言，其受命也如響，无有遠近幽深，遂知來物。非天下之至精，其孰能與於此！

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-02
original.text: 參伍以變，錯綜其數，通其變，遂成天下之文，極其數，遂定天下之象；非天下之至變，其孰能與於此！

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-03
original.text: 易，无思也，无為也，寂然不動，感而遂通天下之故。非天下之至神，其孰能與於此！

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-04
original.text: 夫易，聖人之所以極深而研幾也！唯深也，故能通天下之志；唯幾也，故能成天下之務；唯神也，故不疾而速，不行而至。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-05
original.text: 子曰「易有聖人之道四焉」者，此之謂也。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-11-01
original.text: 子曰：「夫易，何為者也？夫易，開物成務，冒天下之道，如斯而已者也。」是故聖人以通天下之志，以定天下之業，以斷天下之疑。是故蓍之德圓而神，卦之德方以知，六爻之義易以貢；聖人以此洗心，退藏於密，吉凶與民同患，神以知來，知以藏往，其孰能與此哉？古之聦明叡知神武而不殺者夫！是以明於天之道，而察於民之故，是興神物以前民用；聖人以此齊戒以神明其德夫！是故闔戶謂之坤，闢戶謂之乾，一闔一闢謂之變；往來不窮謂之通，見乃謂之象，形乃謂之器，制而用之謂之法，利用出入，民咸用之謂之神。是故易有太極，是生兩儀，兩儀生四象，四象生八卦，八卦定吉凶，吉凶生大業。是故法象莫大乎天地；變通莫大乎四時；縣象著明莫大乎日月；崇高莫大乎富貴；備物致用，立成器以為天下利，莫大乎聖人；探賾索隱，鉤深致遠，以定天下之吉凶，成天下之亹亹者，莫大乎蓍龜。是故天生神物，聖人則之。天地變化，聖人效之。天垂象，見吉凶，聖人象之。河出圖，洛出書，聖人則之。易有四象，所以示也。繫辭焉，所以告也。定之以吉凶，所以斷也。

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-12-01
original.text: 易曰：「自天祐之，吉无不利」。子曰：「祐者，助也。天之所助者，順也。人之所助者，信也。履信思乎順，又以尚賢也，是以『自天祐之，吉无不利。』也。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-12-02
original.text: 子曰：「書不盡言，言不盡意。」然則聖人之意，其不可見乎？子曰：「聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情偽，繫辭以盡其言，變而通之以盡利，鼓之舞之以盡神。」

original.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-12-03
original.text: 乾坤，其易之縕邪！乾坤成列，而易立乎其中矣。乾坤毀，則无以見易，易不可見，則乾坤或幾乎息矣。是故形而上者謂之道，形而下者謂之器，化而裁之謂之變，推而行之謂之通，舉而錯之天下之民謂之事業。是故夫象，聖人有以見天下之賾，而擬諸其形容，象其物宜，是故謂之象。聖人有以見天下之動，而觀其會通，以行其典禮，繫辭焉以斷其吉凶，是故謂之爻。極天下之賾者存乎卦；鼓天下之動者存乎辭；化而裁之存乎變；推而行之存乎通；神而明之，存乎其人；默而成之，不言而信，存乎德行。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-01-01
original.text: 八卦成列，象在其中矣；因而重之，爻在其中矣；剛柔相推，變在其中矣；繫辭焉而命之，動在其中矣。吉凶悔吝者，生乎動者也。剛柔者，立本者也；變通者，趣時者也；吉凶者，貞勝者也。天地之道，貞觀者也；日月之道，貞明者也；天下之動，貞夫一者也。夫乾，確然示人易矣；夫坤，隤然示人簡矣。爻也者，效此者也；象也者，像此者也。爻象動乎內，吉凶見乎外，功業見乎變，聖人之情見乎辭。天地之大德曰生，聖人之大寶曰位，何以守位曰仁，何以聚人曰財，理財正辭，禁民為非曰義。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-01
original.text: 古者包犧氏之王天下也，仰則觀象於天，俯則觀法於地，觀鳥獸之文，與地之宜，近取諸身，遠取諸物；於是始作八卦，以通神明之德，以類萬物之情。作結繩而為罔罟，以佃以漁，蓋取諸離。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-02
original.text: 包犧氏沒，神農氏作，斲木為耜，揉木為耒，耒耨之利，以教天下，蓋取諸益。日中為市，致天下之民，聚天下之貨，交易而退，各得其所，蓋取諸噬嗑。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-03
original.text: 神農氏沒，黃帝、堯、舜氏作，通其變，使民不倦；神而化之，使民宜之；易窮則變，變則通，通則久；是以自天祐之，吉无不利。黃帝、堯、舜垂衣裳而天下治，蓋取諸乾坤。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-04
original.text: 刳木為舟，剡木為楫，舟楫之利以濟不通，致遠以利天下，蓋取諸渙。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-05
original.text: 服牛乘馬，引重致遠以利天下，蓋取諸隨。重門擊柝以待暴客，蓋取諸豫。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-06
original.text: 斷木為杵，掘地為臼，臼杵之利，萬民以濟，蓋取諸小過。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-07
original.text: 弦木為弧，剡木為矢，弧矢之利，以威天下，蓋取諸睽。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-08
original.text: 上古穴居而野處，後世聖人易之以宮室，上棟下宇，以待風雨，蓋取諸大壯。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-09
original.text: 古之葬者，厚衣之以薪，葬之中野，不封不樹，喪期无數，後世聖人易之以棺槨，蓋取諸大過。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-10
original.text: 上古結繩而治，後世聖人易之以書契，百官以治，萬民以察，蓋取諸周易/夬。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-03-01
original.text: 是故易者，象也。象也者，像也。彖者，材也。爻也者，效天下之動者也。是故吉凶生而悔吝著也。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-03-02
original.text: 陽卦多陰，陰卦多陽，其故何也？陽卦奇，陰卦偶。其德行何也？陽一君而二民，君子之道也；陰二君而一民，小人之道也。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-01
original.text: 易曰：「憧憧往來，朋從爾思。」子曰：「天下何思何慮！天下同歸而殊途，一致而百慮，天下何思何慮！日往則月來，月往則日來，日月相推而明生焉。寒往則暑來，暑往則寒來，寒暑相推而歲成焉。往者，屈也；來者，信也。屈信相感而利生焉。尺蠖之屈，以求信也。龍蛇之蟄，以存身也。精義入神，以致用也。利用安身，以崇德也。過此以往，未之或知也。窮神知化，德之盛也。」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-02
original.text: 易曰：「困于石，據于蒺蔾，入于其宮，不見其妻，凶。」子曰：「非所困而困焉，名必辱；非所據而據焉，身必危；既辱且危，死期將至，妻其可得見耶！」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-03
original.text: 易曰：「公用射隼于高墉之上，獲之，无不利。」子曰：「隼者，禽也；弓矢者，器也。射之者，人也。君子藏器於身，待時而動，何不利之有。動而不括，是以出而有獲，語成器而動者也。」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-04
original.text: 子曰：「小人不恥不仁，不畏不義，不見利不勸，不威不懲，小懲而大誡，此小人之福也。易曰：『履校滅趾，无咎。』此之謂也。善不積不足以成名，惡不積不足以滅身，小人以小善為无益而弗為也，以小惡為无傷而弗去也；故惡積而不可揜，罪大而不可解。易曰：『何校滅耳，凶。』」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-05
original.text: 子曰：「危者，安其位者也。亡者，保其存者也。亂者，有其治者也。是故君子安而不忘危，存而不忘亡，治而不忘亂，是以身安而國家可保也。易曰：『其亡其亡，繫于苞桑。』」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-06
original.text: 子曰：「德薄而位尊，知小而謀大，力小而任重，鮮不及矣。易曰：『鼎折足，覆公餗，其形渥，凶。』言不勝其任也。」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-07
original.text: 子曰：「知幾其神乎！君子上交不諂，下交不瀆，其知幾乎！幾者，動之微，吉之先見者也。君子見幾而作，不俟終日。易曰：『介于石，不終日，貞吉。』介如石焉，寧用終日，斷可識矣。君子知微知彰，知柔知剛，萬夫之望。」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-08
original.text: 子曰：「顏氏之子，其殆庶幾乎！有不善，未嘗不知；知之，未嘗復行也。易曰：『不遠復，无祇悔，元吉。』天地絪縕，萬物化醇；男女構精，萬物化生。易曰：『三人行，則損一人；一人行，則得其友。』言致一也。」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-09
original.text: 子曰：「君子安其身而後動，易其心而後語，定其交而後求。君子脩此三者，故全也。危以動，則民不與也。懼以語，則民不應也。无交而求，則民不與也。莫之與，則傷之者至矣。易曰：『莫益之，或擊之。立心勿恒，凶。』」

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-05-01
original.text: 子曰：「乾坤，其易之門邪！乾，陽物也；坤，陰物也。陰陽合德，而剛柔有體，以體天地之撰，以通神明之德。」其稱名也，雜而不越，於稽其類，其衰世之意邪！夫易，彰往而察來，而微顯闡幽，開而當名辨物，正言斷辭，則備矣。其稱名也小，其取類也大，其旨遠，其辭文，其言曲而中，其事肆而隱，因貳以濟民行，以明失得之報。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-01
original.text: 易之興也，其於中古乎！作易者，其有憂患乎！是故：

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-02
original.text: 履，德之基也。謙，德之柄也。復，德之本也。恒，德之固也。損，德之脩也。益，德之裕也。困，德之辨也。井，德之地也。巽，德之制也。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-03
original.text: 履，和而至。謙，尊而光。復，小而辨於物。恒，雜而不厭。損，先難而後易。益，長裕而不没。困，窮而通。井，居其所而遷。巽，稱而隱。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-04
original.text: 履，以和行。謙，以制禮。復，以自知。恒，以一德。損，以遠害。益，以興利。困，以寡怨。井，以辯義。巽，以行權。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-07-01
original.text: 易之為書也不可遠，為道也屢遷；變動不居，周流六虛，上下无常，剛柔相易，不可為典要，唯變所適。其出入以度，外內使知懼。又明於憂患與故，无有師保，如臨父母。初率其辭而揆其方，既有典常，苟非其人，道不虛行。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-07-02
original.text: 易之為書也，原始要終以為質也。六爻相雜，唯其時物也。其初難知，其上易知，本末也。初辭擬之，卒成之終。若夫雜物撰德，辨是與非，則非其中爻不備。噫，亦要存亡吉凶，則居可知矣。知者觀其彖辭，則思過半矣。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-08-01
original.text: 二與四同功而異位，其善不同：二多譽，四多懼，近也。柔之為道，不利近者，其要無咎，其用柔中也。三與五同功而異位，其遇不同：三多凶，五多功，貴賤之等也。其柔危，其剛勝邪？

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-08-02
original.text: 《易》之為書也，廣大悉備：有天道焉，有人道焉，有地道焉，兼三材而兩之，故六。六者，非它也，三材之道也。道有變動，故曰爻；爻有等，故曰物；物相雜，故曰文；文不當，故吉凶生焉。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-08-03
original.text: 《易》之興也，其當殷之末世，周之盛德邪！當文王與紂之事邪！是故其辭危，危者使平，易者使傾，其道甚大，百物不廢，懼以終始，其要无咎；此之謂易之道也。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-09-01
original.text: 夫乾，天下之至健也；德行恒易以知險。夫坤，天下之至順也；德行恒簡以知阻。能說諸心，能研諸侯之慮，定天下之吉凶，成天下之亹亹者。是故變化云為，吉事有祥，象事知器，占事知來。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-09-02
original.text: 天地設位，聖人成能；人謀鬼謀，百姓與能。八卦以象告，爻彖以情言，剛柔雜居，而吉凶可見矣。變動以利言，吉凶以情遷。是故愛惡相攻而吉凶生，遠近相取而悔吝生，情偽相感而利害生。凡易之情，近而不相得，則凶或害之，悔且吝。

original.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-09-03
original.text: 將叛者其辭慚，中心疑者其辭枝；吉人之辭寡，躁人之辭多；誣善之人其辭游，失其守者其辭屈。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-01-01
original.text: 昔者，聖人之作《易》也，幽贊於神明而生蓍。參天兩地而倚數，觀變於陰陽而立卦；發揮於剛柔而生爻；和順於道德而理於義；窮理盡性以至於命。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-02-01
original.text: 昔者，聖人之作《易》也，將以順性命之理。是以立天之道，曰陰與陽；立地之道，曰柔與剛；立人之道，曰仁與義。兼三才而兩之，故易六畫而成卦。分陰分陽，迭用柔剛，故易六位而成章。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-03-01
original.text: 天地定位，山澤通氣，雷風相薄，水火不相射。八卦相錯，數往者順，知來者逆。是故易逆數也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-04-01
original.text: 雷以動之，風以散之，雨以潤之，日以烜之，艮以止之，兌以說之，乾以君之，坤以藏之。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-01
original.text: 帝出乎震，齊乎巽，相見乎離，致役乎坤，說言乎兌，戰乎乾，勞乎坎，成言乎艮。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-02
original.text: 萬物出乎震，震，東方也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-03
original.text: 齊乎巽，巽，東南也，齊也者，言萬物之潔齊也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-04
original.text: 離也者，明也，萬物皆相見，南方之卦也。聖人南面而聽天下，嚮明而治，蓋取諸此也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-05
original.text: 坤也者，地也，萬物皆致養焉，故曰致役乎坤。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-06
original.text: 兌，正秋也。萬物之所說也。故曰說；言乎兌。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-07
original.text: 戰乎乾，乾，西北之卦也。言陰陽相薄也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-08
original.text: 坎者，水也，正北方之卦也，勞卦也，萬物之所歸也，故曰勞乎坎。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-09
original.text: 艮，東北之卦也，萬物之所成，終而所成始也，故曰成言乎艮。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-01
original.text: 神也者。妙萬物而為言者也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-02
original.text: 動萬物者，莫疾乎雷。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-03
original.text: 橈萬物者，莫疾乎風。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-04
original.text: 燥萬物者，莫熯乎火。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-05
original.text: 說萬物者，莫說乎澤。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-06
original.text: 潤萬物者，莫潤乎水。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-07
original.text: 終萬物、始萬物者，莫盛乎艮。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-08
original.text: 故水火相逮，雷風不相悖，山澤通氣，然後能變化，既成萬物也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-07-01
original.text: 乾，健也。坤，順也。震，動也。巽，入也。坎，陷也。離，麗也。艮，止也。兌，說也。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-08-01
original.text: 乾為馬，坤為牛，震為龍，巽為雞，坎為豕，離為雉，艮為狗，兌為羊。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-09-01
original.text: 乾為首，坤為腹，震為足，巽為股，坎為耳，離為目，艮為手，兌為口。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-10-01
original.text: 乾，天也，故稱乎父；坤，地也，故稱乎母；震一索而得男，故謂之長男；巽一索而得女，故謂之長女；坎再索而得男，故謂之中男；離再索而得女，故謂之中女；艮三索而得男，故謂之少男；兌三索而得女，故謂之少女。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-01
original.text: 乾為天、為圜、為君、為父、為玉、為金、為寒、為冰、為大赤、為良馬、為老馬、為瘠馬、為駁馬、為木果。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-02
original.text: 坤為地、為母、為布、為釜、為吝嗇、為均、為子母牛、為大輿、為文、為眾、為柄。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-03
original.text: 其於地也為黑。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-04
original.text: 震為雷、為龍、為玄黃、為敷、為大涂、為長子、為決躁、為蒼筤竹、為萑葦。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-05
original.text: 其於馬也，為善鳴、為馵足，為的顙。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-06
original.text: 其於稼也，為反生。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-07
original.text: 其究為健，為蕃鮮。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-08
original.text: 巽為木、為風、為長女、為繩直、為工、為白、為長、為高、為進退、為不果、為臭。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-09
original.text: 其於人也，為寡髮、為廣顙、為多白眼、為近利市三倍。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-10
original.text: 其究為躁卦。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-11
original.text: 坎為水、為溝瀆、為隱伏、為矯輮、為弓輪。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-12
original.text: 其於人也，為加憂、為心病、為耳痛、為血卦、為赤。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-13
original.text: 其於馬也，為美脊、為亟心、為下首、為薄蹄、為曳。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-14
original.text: 其於輿也，為多眚、為通、為月、為盜。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-15
original.text: 其於木也，為堅多心。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-16
original.text: 離為火、為日、為電、為中女、為甲冑、為戈兵。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-17
original.text: 其於人也，為大腹、為乾卦、為鱉、為蟹、為蠃、為蚌、為龜。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-18
original.text: 其於木也，為科上槁。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-19
original.text: 艮為山、為徑路、為小石、為門闕、為果蓏、為閽寺、為指、為狗、為鼠、為黔喙之屬。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-20
original.text: 其於木也，為堅多節。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-21
original.text: 兌為澤、為少女、為巫、為口舌、為毀折、為附決。

original.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-22
original.text: 其於地也，為剛鹵，為妾、為羊。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-01
original.text: 有天地，然後萬物生焉。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-02
original.text: 盈天地之間者，唯萬物，故受之以屯；屯者盈也，屯者物之始生也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-03
original.text: 物生必蒙，故受之以蒙；蒙者蒙也，物之穉也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-04
original.text: 物穉不可不養也，故受之以需；需者飲食之道也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-05
original.text: 飲食必有訟，故受之以訟。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-06
original.text: 訟必有眾起，故受之以師；師者眾也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-07
original.text: 眾必有所比，故受之以比；比者比也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-08
original.text: 比必有所畜也，故受之以小畜。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-09
original.text: 物畜然後有禮，故受之以履。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-10
original.text: 履而泰，然後安，故受之以泰；泰者通也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-11
original.text: 物不可以終通，故受之以否。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-12
original.text: 物不可以終否，故受之以同人。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-13
original.text: 與人同者，物必歸焉，故受之以大有。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-14
original.text: 有大者不可以盈，故受之以謙。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-15
original.text: 有大而能謙，必豫，故受之以豫。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-16
original.text: 豫必有隨，故受之以隨。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-17
original.text: 以喜隨人者，必有事，故受之以蠱；蠱者事也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-18
original.text: 有事而后可大，故受之以臨；臨者大也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-19
original.text: 物大然後可觀，故受之以觀。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-20
original.text: 可觀而后有所合，故受之以噬嗑；嗑者合也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-21
original.text: 物不可以苟合而已，故受之以賁；賁者飾也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-22
original.text: 致飾然後亨，則盡矣，故受之以剝；剝者剝也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-23
original.text: 物不可以終盡，剝窮上反下，故受之以復。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-24
original.text: 復則不妄矣，故受之以无妄。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-25
original.text: 有无妄然後可畜，故受之以大畜。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-26
original.text: 物畜然後可養，故受之以頤；頤者養也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-27
original.text: 不養則不可動，故受之以大過。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-28
original.text: 物不可以終過，故受之以坎；坎者陷也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-29
original.text: 陷必有所麗，故受之以離；離者麗也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-01
original.text: 有天地然後有萬物，有萬物然後有男女，有男女然後有夫婦，有夫婦然後有父子，有父子然後有君臣，有君臣然後有上下，有上下然後禮儀有所錯。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-02
original.text: 夫婦之道，不可以不久也，故受之以恆；恆者久也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-03
original.text: 物不可以久居其所，故受之以遯；遯者退也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-04
original.text: 物不可終遯，故受之以大壯。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-05
original.text: 物不可以終壯，故受之以晉；晉者進也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-06
original.text: 進必有所傷，故受之以明夷；夷者傷也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-07
original.text: 傷於外者，必反其家，故受之以家人。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-08
original.text: 家道窮必乖，故受之以睽；睽者乖也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-09
original.text: 乖必有難，故受之以蹇；蹇者難也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-10
original.text: 物不可終難，故受之以解；解者緩也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-11
original.text: 緩必有所失，故受之以損。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-12
original.text: 損而不已，必益，故受之以益。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-13
original.text: 益而不已，必決，故受之以夬；夬者決也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-14
original.text: 決必有所遇，故受之以姤；姤者遇也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-15
original.text: 物相遇而后聚，故受之以萃；萃者聚也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-16
original.text: 聚而上者，謂之升，故受之以升。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-17
original.text: 升而不已，必困，故受之以困。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-18
original.text: 困乎上者，必反下，故受之以井。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-19
original.text: 井道不可不革，故受之以革。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-20
original.text: 革物者莫若鼎，故受之以鼎。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-21
original.text: 主器者莫若長子，故受之以震；震者動也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-22
original.text: 物不可以終動，止之，故受之以艮；艮者止也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-23
original.text: 物不可以終止，故受之以漸；漸者進也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-24
original.text: 進必有所歸，故受之以歸妹。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-25
original.text: 得其所歸者必大，故受之以豐；豐者大也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-26
original.text: 窮大者必失其居，故受之以旅。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-27
original.text: 旅而無所容，故受之以巽；巽者入也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-28
original.text: 入而后說之，故受之以兌；兌者說也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-29
original.text: 說而后散之，故受之以渙；渙者離也。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-30
original.text: 物不可以終離，故受之以節。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-31
original.text: 節而信之，故受之以中孚。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-32
original.text: 有其信者，必行之，故受之以小過。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-33
original.text: 有過物者，必濟，故受之既濟。

original.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-34
original.text: 物不可窮也，故受之以未濟；終焉。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-01
original.text: 乾剛坤柔，比樂師憂。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-02
original.text: 臨、觀之義，或與或求。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-03
original.text: 屯見而不失其居，蒙雜而著。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-04
original.text: 震起也，艮止也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-05
original.text: 損、益，盛衰之始也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-06
original.text: 大畜時也，无妄災也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-07
original.text: 萃聚，而升不來也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-08
original.text: 謙輕，而豫怠也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-09
original.text: 噬嗑食也，賁无色也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-10
original.text: 兌見，而巽伏也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-11
original.text: 隨无故也，蠱則飭也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-12
original.text: 剝爛也，復反也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-13
original.text: 晉晝也，明夷誅也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-14
original.text: 井通，而困相遇也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-15
original.text: 咸速也，恒久也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-16
original.text: 渙離也，節止也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-17
original.text: 解緩也，蹇難也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-18
original.text: 睽外也，家人內也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-19
original.text: 否、泰，反其類也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-20
original.text: 大壯則止，遯則退也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-21
original.text: 大有眾也，同人親也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-22
original.text: 革去故也，鼎取新也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-23
original.text: 小過過也，中孚信也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-24
original.text: 豐多故也，親寡旅也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-25
original.text: 離上，而坎下也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-26
original.text: 小畜寡也，履不處也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-27
original.text: 需不進也，訟不親也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-28
original.text: 大過顛也，姤遇也，柔遇剛也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-29
original.text: 漸女歸待男行也，頤養正也，既濟定也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-30
original.text: 歸妹女之終也，未濟男之窮也。

original.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-31
original.text: 夬決也，剛決柔也。君子道長，小人道消也。

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-01-01
translation.text: The Qian commentary describes the immense creative power of Heaven. All things receive their beginnings from it; clouds move, rain falls, and living forms take shape. The six lines are compared to six dragons moving with the proper times. As the heavenly way changes, each being develops according to its own nature while participating in a larger harmony. The passage ends by connecting this creative order with peace among the many states.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-02-01
translation.text: The Kun commentary describes Earth as receptive, spacious, and sustaining. It carries and nourishes all living things by responding to Heaven rather than competing for leadership. The image of a mare conveys endurance and gentle perseverance. A noble person who insists on leading first may lose the way; one who follows the appropriate course finds direction. The references to southwest and northeast, companions and separation, emphasize the importance of position, relationship, and steadfastness.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-03-01
translation.text: Zhun concerns the difficulties of a beginning. Firm and yielding forces first meet, producing both the possibility of growth and immediate obstacles. Thunder and rain fill an unsettled world that has not yet found its order. The commentary does not treat the difficulty as a reason to abandon everything. Instead, it urges the establishment of leadership and organization while recognizing that the work of founding a stable order cannot be completed in comfort or haste.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-04-01
translation.text: Meng describes ignorance as a condition in which danger is encountered and movement comes to a stop. Yet confusion can be transformed through education when teacher and student respond sincerely to each other. The learner must seek instruction rather than expect it to be imposed. A serious first question deserves an answer, whereas repeated disrespectful questioning undermines the relationship. Cultivating correctness from the beginning is presented as one of education’s most important achievements.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-05-01
translation.text: Xu means waiting because danger lies ahead. Firm strength does not have to charge into a trap; its strength is shown by remaining steady without becoming trapped. Sincerity, clarity, and a central, appropriate position make waiting purposeful rather than passive. The reference to crossing a great river suggests that action can succeed when the conditions are right. The lesson is to distinguish deliberate preparation from fearful avoidance and reckless advance.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-06-01
translation.text: Song concerns disputes arising when danger and forceful assertion come together. Even a person who believes the claim is sincere may encounter obstruction and must remain alert. Stopping the argument before it becomes absolute is preferable to pursuing victory at any cost. The commentary praises an impartial and balanced authority and warns against undertaking a hazardous venture during conflict. Winning an endless quarrel is not the same as resolving it well.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-07-01
translation.text: Shi refers to a multitude, particularly an army. The commentary connects legitimate command with correctness: a leader must direct the people toward a defensible purpose. Firmness in the central position is matched by the capacity to secure support. Military action is dangerous and causes suffering, yet its outcome is described as favorable when it is disciplined and undertaken for a proper cause. This is a statement of an ancient political ideal, not a modern endorsement of warfare.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-08-01
translation.text: Bi describes people drawing together and offering one another support. Good association requires a trustworthy center and a commitment that can last. People who feel insecure are drawn toward dependable leadership, while those who delay their response may lose the opportunity to join. The commentary explains the favorable judgment through mutual responsiveness between upper and lower positions. Closeness is valuable when it rests on constancy and appropriate relationships.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-09-01
translation.text: Xiao Xu presents the accumulation of influence through a relatively small and yielding force. One yielding line occupies an effective position and receives the response of stronger lines. Inner strength works together with outward gentleness so that intentions can gradually be realized. Thick clouds gather without producing rain: the potential is there, but its benefits have not yet appeared. The image emphasizes restraint, accumulation, and the difference between preparation and fruition.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-10-01
translation.text: Lü concerns conduct under demanding conditions. A yielding force moves among stronger ones, and pleasure or harmony responds to the firmness of Heaven. For that reason, walking on a tiger’s tail does not necessarily end in a bite. Success comes through behavior that is appropriately measured rather than merely timid. The commentary also describes firm, centered leadership as bright and free from inward reproach, connecting conduct with moral responsibility.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-11-01
translation.text: Tai portrays free communication between Heaven and Earth and between those above and below. When their influences meet, living things flourish and people can share their purposes. The firm and active principle is within, while the yielding and receptive principle is outside. The language of noble and petty people expresses an ancient moral-political order in which worthy conduct gains influence and destructive conduct loses ground. Prosperity depends on connection, not isolation.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-12-01
translation.text: Pi is the opposite condition: Heaven and Earth cease to exchange their influences, and communication between upper and lower levels fails. The large and constructive principle retreats while the small and obstructive one advances. The commentary pictures a political and social order that cannot function because its parts are disconnected. Worthy people are pushed aside while narrow interests gain strength. The warning concerns the consequences of isolation and the loss of mutual trust.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-13-01
translation.text: Tong Ren describes fellowship that extends beyond a private faction. A yielding line holds a central position and responds to the strength of Heaven, making common purpose possible. To meet others openly in the fields is to seek cooperation without restricting it to one household or group. Inner clarity and outer strength should be held together through uprightness. The commentary gives the noble person the task of understanding and connecting the aspirations of people throughout the world.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-14-01
translation.text: Da You concerns abundance held in a responsible way. A yielding line occupies the honored central position and receives the response of strong lines above and below. Such abundance is not explained by possessions alone. Firm energy, clarity, and action suited to the proper time allow resources and influence to serve a larger order. The commentary associates great success with receptivity at the center and the support of others.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-15-01
translation.text: Qian explains why modesty can produce lasting achievement. Heaven lowers what is excessive and raises what is humble; Earth also redistributes what accumulates too high. The passage extends this pattern to spirits and human relations, saying that arrogance attracts opposition while humility wins support. A person in a high position becomes brighter through modesty, while a person in a low position gains dignity. Modesty is presented as a durable principle of conduct.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-16-01
translation.text: Yu joins readiness, harmony, and movement that follows the appropriate time. Firm strength receives a response while action proceeds through receptiveness. The commentary compares this with the orderly movement of sun, moon, and seasons. Government and the use of punishment should also follow an intelligible order, allowing people to accept authority. Establishing political leadership or mobilizing an army is discussed within that ancient framework of timing and collective coordination.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-17-01
translation.text: Sui describes following without surrendering judgment. Firm strength places itself beneath the yielding, and movement is accompanied by a sense of ease. People follow because the relationship is responsive rather than merely coercive. The commentary stresses that the wider world changes with time; successful following therefore requires adjustment to circumstances while keeping to the right course. The meaning of timing is at the center of this hexagram.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-18-01
translation.text: Gu concerns the repair of what has become spoiled through neglect. Strong and yielding forces are positioned in a way that combines penetration with stopping, producing accumulated disorder. Yet the commentary treats the resulting problem as an opportunity for restoring order. Crossing a great river means undertaking necessary work. The days before and after the designated turning point suggest preparation, action, and review. An ending may also be a new beginning.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-19-01
translation.text: Lin describes a growing firm force that approaches and exercises influence. Joyful responsiveness and receptive conduct allow correct action to progress. The commentary also recalls a warning about danger in the eighth month: growth does not continue forever, and what is strong can begin to decline. A favorable period is therefore not a reason for complacency. Its value lies in understanding the cycle of increase and decrease.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-20-01
translation.text: Guan is about observation and the influence of an example. Those in prominent positions should view the world with receptiveness, humility, and fairness. The ritual image of washing before the offering portrays a solemn attitude that invites respect even before the ceremony is complete. The commentary also considers the regular movement of the seasons. From such patterns, it explains how moral instruction can emerge through visible conduct rather than force alone.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-21-01
translation.text: Shi He describes a blockage that must be bitten through before communication can resume. Firm and yielding forces are distinct, and vigorous movement is joined with clear perception, like thunder together with lightning. The commentary applies this image to deciding judicial cases, where determination must be matched by understanding. It is an ancient account of punishment and legal order, not a license for arbitrary severity.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-22-01
translation.text: Bi concerns ornament, pattern, and culture. Yielding and firm forces decorate or temper one another, producing a limited but genuine capacity for progress. The patterned interplay of forces is called the order of Heaven; cultivated clarity and restraint become the order of human affairs. By observing natural patterns, people recognize changes in season and time. By attending to human culture, they develop customs and forms of education that shape social life.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-23-01
translation.text: Bo portrays a process of stripping away. Yielding forces steadily replace the firm, making forward movement unwise. The commentary advises recognizing this tendency and knowing when to stop. The noble person observes increase and decline, fullness and emptiness, as recurring features of the natural order. When a structure is losing its support, forcing progress may only deepen its instability.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-24-01
translation.text: Fu describes the return of firm, life-giving energy. Movement begins again and proceeds in a receptive way, so coming and going need not cause harm. The image of return after seven days expresses a recurring rhythm rather than a fixed promise of immediate success. The commentary associates the moment with growth and asks whether the renewal of life reveals something of the heart of Heaven and Earth.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-25-01
translation.text: Wu Wang means acting without falsehood or reckless intention. Firm strength enters and becomes the central influence, joining movement with vigor. Appropriate action is described as aligned with the order of Heaven. Yet an act that departs from correctness invites trouble, even if it appears energetic. The commentary questions the value of proceeding when conduct no longer agrees with the right course.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-26-01
translation.text: Da Xu concerns the storing and disciplining of great strength. Firmness, substantiality, and brightness are joined with daily renewal of character. The ability to restrain force is itself a major form of correctness. Honoring capable people and supporting their service beyond the private household bring the strength to public use. Crossing a great river represents undertaking significant work with resources and timing properly aligned.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-27-01
translation.text: Yi examines nourishment in both its material and ethical senses. To nourish rightly means observing what is supported and how a person provides for themselves. Heaven and Earth sustain living things; a wise ruler supports the capable and cares for the wider population. The commentary treats nourishment as a serious responsibility: what people feed, cultivate, and maintain reveals their values.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-28-01
translation.text: Da Guo describes a situation whose burden has exceeded its ordinary support. A roof beam bends because its ends are weak even though the middle is strong. The commentary does not say that all action must stop. Firmness can still be balanced by a yielding manner and a readiness to meet others. Extraordinary pressure calls for extraordinary discernment, especially about whether the supporting structure can bear the weight.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-29-01
translation.text: Kan concerns repeated danger. Flowing water enters difficult places without losing its nature, offering an image of faithfulness under pressure. Inner strength remains central, and successful action requires an honest understanding of risk. The commentary also considers natural barriers in the sky and landscape, along with defensive works established by rulers. Danger must be understood, navigated, and sometimes used for protection.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary I / TUAN-U TUAN-U-30-01
translation.text: Li means attachment or dependence. The sun and moon are attached to Heaven, while grasses and grains depend on Earth. Light achieves its purpose when it is connected to what is right. A yielding line in a central and correct position allows clarity to operate without harshness. The image of raising a gentle cow connects successful cultivation with patient, receptive steadiness.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-31-01
translation.text: Xian means mutual influence or response. Yielding and firm forces meet, and the two energies affect one another. Stillness combines with joy, and the man’s deferential approach to the woman belongs to the passage’s ancient marriage symbolism. The commentary broadens the theme: Heaven and Earth respond and produce life; wise people respond to human feeling and support peace. Observing relationships reveals how beings influence one another.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-32-01
translation.text: Heng means continuity. Thunder and wind work together, while firm and yielding lines find their counterparts. Constancy is not mere immobility; it is commitment to a right course through continuing change. The sun and moon shine through regular movement, and the seasons complete their cycles by changing. The commentary asks what a person remains faithful to over time, since duration has value only when it serves an appropriate principle.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-33-01
translation.text: Dun concerns withdrawal at the proper time. Retreat is not automatically defeat: it may be the very means of preserving a worthwhile course. Firm strength still occupies an appropriate position, but a growing yielding influence alters the circumstances. Small matters can remain stable while broader confrontation becomes unwise. The commentary highlights the importance of recognizing when to step back.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-34-01
translation.text: Da Zhuang describes strength at its height. Firm energy is capable of decisive movement, but true greatness requires righteousness. The commentary rejects the assumption that power alone makes an action appropriate. Its final statement connects what is great and upright with the deeper character of Heaven and Earth.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-35-01
translation.text: Jin means advancement. Brightness rises above the Earth, and receptive conduct aligns itself with what is illuminating. A yielding line rises into an influential position. The narrative of a lord receiving horses and frequent audiences with the king illustrates recognition and promotion in an ancient political setting. Advancement is meaningful when it follows clarity and responsive conduct.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-36-01
translation.text: Ming Yi depicts light going beneath the Earth and becoming obscured. Inner clarity may need to be protected by outward modesty during great hardship. The commentary invokes King Wen and Jizi as figures who endured danger without abandoning their inner commitments. Difficulty is not interpreted as a reason to surrender correctness; sometimes wisdom requires keeping one’s light out of view.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-37-01
translation.text: Jia Ren discusses order within a household through the roles recognized by ancient society. Its statements about men and women reflect historical family arrangements rather than a universal modern rule. Parents are expected to guide the family, and each relationship carries responsibilities. The commentary connects orderly family conduct with the stability of the larger political community.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-38-01
translation.text: Kui concerns difference and separation. Fire moves upward while water in the marsh moves downward, suggesting directions that do not naturally coincide. Even people who share a home may have different purposes. The commentary nevertheless points out that Heaven and Earth remain jointly productive despite differences. The lesson is not that all distinctions disappear, but that a limited form of cooperation may still be possible.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-39-01
translation.text: Jian means obstruction. Danger lies ahead, and the ability to stop upon recognizing it is called wisdom. The directions southwest and northeast symbolize different degrees of practical difficulty. Seeking the help of a capable person and preserving the right position are both praised. The passage places discernment and support above stubborn persistence.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-40-01
translation.text: Jie describes release from difficulty through timely movement. After a danger has been resolved, returning to an ordinary position can be fortunate; when necessary tasks remain, acting early can produce results. The commentary compares release to thunder and rain breaking a period of confinement, allowing plants to emerge and grow. Removing an obstruction restores possibilities that had been held back.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-41-01
translation.text: Sun describes reduction, especially the transfer of resources or influence from below to above. Sincere reduction can be appropriate, but it must occur at the right time and in the right measure. The commentary uses a modest ritual offering to show that simplicity may express genuine reverence. Firmness and yielding, gain and loss, fullness and emptiness are all adjusted in response to the time.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-42-01
translation.text: Yi means increase. The passage describes benefit flowing from above to those below, creating broad satisfaction among the people. Those in authority become more effective when they support others rather than merely accumulate resources. Correct and central action brings favorable results. Just as a boat enables a river crossing, well-directed benefit creates new practical possibilities. Increase should follow changing circumstances.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-43-01
translation.text: Guai describes a decisive break. A strong majority confronts a remaining obstacle, but judgment should be public and truthful rather than driven by aggression. The court and the local community are settings for making the danger known. Resorting immediately to arms is discouraged. The commentary favors a firm but measured resolution of conflict when the time has become ripe.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-44-01
translation.text: Gou means encountering. Yielding and firm forces unexpectedly meet, creating both generative possibility and a warning about allowing one influence to grow unchecked. The marriage language belongs to the traditional symbolism of the text. The commentary also observes that Heaven and Earth meet and living things take form. What matters is the character and consequence of an encounter.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-45-01
translation.text: Cui means gathering. People come together when receptive conduct, mutual pleasure, and a reliable center work in concert. The ruler’s visit to an ancestral temple is an image of shared ritual and common belonging. Yet gathering must serve a proper purpose and recognize legitimate leadership. The commentary invites attention not only to the number of people assembled but also to what draws them together.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-46-01
translation.text: Sheng means rising or gradual ascent. Yielding strength advances according to its time, supported by modest conduct and a strong central response. Visiting a capable leader is favorable; movement toward the south symbolizes a purposeful journey. The commentary understands growth as something achieved by steady alignment, not by forceful self-promotion.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-47-01
translation.text: Kun describes confinement, especially the obscuring of firm strength. A person can still preserve an inner sense of rightness while facing severe constraints. The commentary praises the noble person who remains true to position and principle. A central, firm character matters more than an abundance of explanations, for words alone cannot restore trust when circumstances have become difficult.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-48-01
translation.text: Jing uses the image of a well. A town may change, but the well continues to nourish those who come and go. The essential resource remains useful only if it can be drawn and shared. An unfinished draw or a broken vessel defeats the effort just before success. The commentary distinguishes enduring public value from the practical work required to make that value accessible.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-49-01
translation.text: Ge describes transformation when opposed forces can no longer remain as they are. Water and fire conflict, suggesting a need for change. Reform gains trust only when its time has arrived. The commentary links rightful change with the turning of the seasons and with ancient political revolutions. Change without legitimacy is unstable; change undertaken at the proper time can resolve regret.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-50-01
translation.text: Ding uses the ritual cooking vessel as an image of nourishment and ordered transformation. Wood feeds fire, and the vessel prepares offerings for the divine and food for worthy people. The commentary links receptive intelligence with an effective central position. Great success comes not from the vessel itself but from the proper use of resources in service of ritual and community.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-51-01
translation.text: Zhen means shaking or thunder. Sudden fear can become the beginning of care and good fortune if it leads to disciplined conduct. After the shock, one may recover enough composure to speak and laugh. The thunder that startles distant and nearby people becomes an image of leadership able to maintain its duties even under disturbance.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-52-01
translation.text: Gen means stopping. The appropriate action is not always motion: there are times to halt and times to proceed. True clarity depends on acting and resting at the right moment. The commentary describes stopping where one should stop and letting go of self-centered attachment. The absence of mutual entanglement between the lines makes freedom from blame possible.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-53-01
translation.text: Jian, meaning gradual progress, likens orderly advancement to a marriage conducted according to accepted rites. Reaching the proper position makes constructive achievement possible. Inner stillness and outward gentleness allow progress without exhaustion. The text connects personal development and public order through the idea that a stable result requires a suitable process.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-54-01
translation.text: Gui Mei treats marriage and the continuation of generations as a major relationship between Heaven, Earth, and humanity. Yet the marriage described here is marked by problematic positions and an imbalance between yielding and firm forces. Acting simply because one is pleased does not guarantee a good outcome. The commentary reflects ancient marriage conventions while examining the consequences of a relationship entered under unsuitable conditions.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-55-01
translation.text: Feng means abundance or greatness. Brightness joined with vigorous movement produces a flourishing condition. A ruler at the height of prosperity is compared to the midday sun, whose light reaches far. Yet the very same image also warns that the sun must decline after noon and the full moon must wane. Prosperity and change are inseparable.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-56-01
translation.text: Lü concerns the traveler, who lacks a fixed home and has only limited resources. A yielding line occupies the central position outside, cooperating with firm strength. Stillness and attachment to clarity permit modest progress. A traveler can act successfully by remaining correct and cautious, but the situation is not the same as secure residence.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-57-01
translation.text: Xun describes repeated penetration and the careful transmission of instructions. Firm strength remains responsive to central correctness, while yielding lines cooperate with it. The result is limited but workable progress. Seeing a capable person and undertaking measured action are favorable because influence grows through persistence and clarity rather than sudden force.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-58-01
translation.text: Dui means joy and openness. Firmness is held within while yielding appears outwardly, so pleasant conduct need not abandon principle. When leaders foster confidence and shared purpose, people may willingly undertake work and face hardship. The commentary presents joy as a powerful social bond when grounded in correctness and genuine human response.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-59-01
translation.text: Huan concerns dispersal and the removal of blockage. Firm strength does not become trapped, and yielding influence finds an appropriate position. The ruler’s temple represents a common center that can reassemble people after division. Crossing a great river by boat illustrates movement made possible by suitable means. Dispersal can therefore clear a path toward renewed connection.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-60-01
translation.text: Jie describes measured limits. Firm and yielding positions are differentiated, while central firmness prevents arbitrary excess. Severe restriction that causes needless suffering cannot last. Proper limits, by contrast, help institutions function and protect resources. Just as the seasons arise through orderly divisions, a good system sets bounds without exhausting wealth or harming the people.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-61-01
translation.text: Zhong Fu concerns inner sincerity. Yielding forces lie within, while firmness occupies central positions; openness and humility make trust effective. The image of even small creatures being reached by sincerity expresses how far integrity may extend. A hollow wooden boat can cross a river, linking inner openness with practical action. Sincerity becomes valuable when joined with correctness.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-62-01
translation.text: Xiao Guo concerns a slight excess that may be acceptable in small matters but dangerous in major ones. Yielding lines occupy central positions while firm lines are poorly placed. The bird in flight symbolizes the risk of rising too high. The commentary recommends lowering one’s aim and adapting to circumstance rather than taking on an undertaking beyond one’s capacity.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-63-01
translation.text: Ji Ji means completion. The lines stand in comparatively appropriate positions, allowing limited success and initial good fortune. Yet completion creates its own danger: if vigilance stops, order may deteriorate into confusion. The commentary cautions that a favorable beginning is not a guarantee of an enduring result.

translation.title: Tuan Commentary II / TUAN-L TUAN-L-64-01
translation.text: Wei Ji means not yet completed. Even without an ideal arrangement of the lines, firm and yielding forces respond to one another. The small fox almost crosses the stream but wets its tail before reaching safety. The image warns against losing care at the final stage. Because completion has not yet been achieved, appropriate effort and mutual response remain necessary.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-01
translation.text: Heaven moves with unflagging strength. A responsible person takes this image as a reason to cultivate character and keep improving without giving up.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-02
translation.text: The hidden dragon should not yet act because the yang line remains at the bottom. Its strength exists, but the appropriate occasion to display it has not arrived.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-03
translation.text: The dragon appearing in the field signifies virtue spreading outward. Worthy conduct is beginning to benefit people beyond the individual.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-04
translation.text: Working diligently throughout the day means repeatedly returning to the proper course. Constant effort must be guided by principles rather than mere activity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-05
translation.text: The dragon poised to leap from the depths can advance without blame. It is beginning to act at the moment when advancement is appropriate.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-06
translation.text: The flying dragon in Heaven signifies the emergence of a capable and virtuous leader. The time has come for such a person to accomplish important work.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-07
translation.text: The dragon soaring too high brings regret because fullness cannot last indefinitely. Excessive ascent, however impressive, eventually meets its limit.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-01-08
translation.text: The use of all nine lines teaches that heavenly virtue does not depend on any one dragon claiming supremacy. Strength is best exercised without a contest for first place.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-01
translation.text: Earth receives and supports everything with its depth and breadth. The exemplary person learns from it to develop generous character and carry the needs of others.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-02
translation.text: The first frost shows that yin has begun to condense. As this small change advances gradually, hard ice will follow; beginnings therefore deserve attention.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-03
translation.text: The movement of the second yin line is straight and square. Its natural conduct is beneficial without rehearsal because the way of Earth is clear and open.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-04
translation.text: Keeping excellence within and remaining steadfast means releasing one’s gifts at the right time. Serving the ruler without claiming achievement shows a broad understanding of duty.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-05
translation.text: Tying up the mouth of the sack avoids blame because careful restraint prevents harm. There are moments when silence offers better protection than display.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-06
translation.text: The yellow lower garment is greatly auspicious because its refinement is held within. Modest appearance can express centered, balanced character.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-07
translation.text: Dragons fighting in the open field show that this course has reached an impasse. When opposing forces become extreme, conflict is difficult to avoid.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-02-08
translation.text: Perseverance in the use of six is favorable because it enables a great completion. Receptive strength fulfils its work through steadfast continuity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-01
translation.text: Clouds and thunder mark the difficulty of beginnings. The exemplary person responds by untangling confusion, organizing affairs, and laying the foundations of good government.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-02
translation.text: Although progress is hesitant, the intention remains directed toward what is right. A person of higher standing gains the people’s support by humbly approaching those below.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-03
translation.text: The difficulty of the second line comes from a yielding line riding a firm one. The long delay before marriage reflects an eventual return to an ordinary, fitting course.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-04
translation.text: Pursuing deer without a guide means chasing prey blindly. The wise person abandons the pursuit because pressing onward would end in frustration.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-05
translation.text: Going forward to seek the marriage shows discernment. The act becomes favorable because the purpose and occasion are finally clear.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-06
translation.text: The rich nourishment cannot yet be shared widely, so its beneficial effects remain limited. Resources alone do not guarantee that help reaches others.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-03-07
translation.text: Tears of blood flow in the final line: how could such distress continue? Endless paralysis and grief cannot provide a sustainable way forward.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-01
translation.text: A spring flows from beneath the mountain. Seeing this image of youthful uncertainty, the exemplary person acts decisively while patiently nurturing moral character.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-02
translation.text: Corrective discipline is useful when it establishes a clear rule. Education should release people from ignorance rather than impose punishment for its own sake.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-03
translation.text: The son’s ability to manage the household arises when firmness and gentleness connect. Successful guidance requires these complementary qualities.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-04
translation.text: The warning against taking the woman concerns conduct that does not proceed in the proper way. Attraction without integrity leads to an unsuitable union.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-05
translation.text: The distress of ignorance results from being isolated from what is real. Refusing instruction and remaining distant from trustworthy knowledge brings regret.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-06
translation.text: The fortunate childlike learner is receptive and modest. Willingness to learn is more valuable than pretending to know everything.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-04-07
translation.text: Defending against bandits succeeds because higher and lower positions cooperate. Proper correction protects people instead of turning force into aggression.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-01
translation.text: Clouds gather above Heaven, but the rain has not yet arrived. The exemplary person waits without agitation, enjoying ordinary food, fellowship, and rest.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-02
translation.text: Waiting in the outskirts avoids entering danger prematurely. Maintaining a steady way of life prevents mistakes and preserves one’s proper course.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-03
translation.text: Waiting on the sand allows room for movement without losing balance. Minor criticism need not spoil an ultimately favorable outcome.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-04
translation.text: Waiting in the mud places one close to trouble; the threat is still outside. If one has attracted attackers, alert and respectful caution may prevent defeat.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-05
translation.text: Waiting amid bloodshed calls for a willingness to heed circumstances. Listening and yielding appropriately offers a path away from immediate peril.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-06
translation.text: Food and drink during the wait are favorable because the person occupies a balanced and proper position. Composure is not the same as neglect.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-05-07
translation.text: Unexpected visitors are treated respectfully, and the ending is fortunate. Though the position is not ideal, the essential requirements have not been seriously lost.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-01
translation.text: Heaven and water move in opposing directions, portraying contention. Before beginning an undertaking, the exemplary person carefully considers its origins and terms.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-02
translation.text: Not prolonging the dispute acknowledges that contention should not endure. Minor objections may arise, but the issues can eventually be clarified.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-03
translation.text: An unsuccessful litigant withdraws and takes refuge. A subordinate who persists in suing a superior readily brings trouble upon himself in this historical setting.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-04
translation.text: Living on inherited virtue and following those above can end favorably. One should undertake service without insistently demanding personal credit.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-05
translation.text: Changing course after a failed dispute means returning to one’s proper obligations. Peaceful constancy keeps a person from greater loss.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-06
translation.text: Judging a lawsuit with great good fortune rests on fairness and balance. Justice requires a decision rooted in what is centered and right.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-06-07
translation.text: An official robe won through litigation is not worthy of honor. A contentious victory does not by itself establish moral respectability.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-01
translation.text: Water lies within Earth, like a gathered force held in reserve. The exemplary person receives the people generously and fosters their shared strength.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-02
translation.text: An army must depart under discipline. When military order breaks down, the expedition risks misfortune, whatever its intentions.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-03
translation.text: Good fortune for the commander comes from receiving the ruler’s trust. Repeated appointments also impose responsibility for protecting the many states.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-04
translation.text: An army returning with corpses has accomplished nothing worthy of praise. Poor command is measured by human loss as well as failure of objectives.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-05
translation.text: Withdrawing and encamping to one side is not blameworthy. A measured retreat need not violate proper military practice.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-06
translation.text: The mature leader commands by the central way; placing an unfit younger man in charge invites casualties. Choosing the wrong commander has grave consequences.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-07-07
translation.text: The great ruler apportions honors to recognize genuine achievement. Unworthy people must not be entrusted with government, lest they disrupt the state.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-01
translation.text: Water spreads over Earth and joins with it. Former kings learned from this image to establish states and maintain close relationships with their regional lords.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-02
translation.text: The first line’s sincere attachment may bring unexpected good fortune. Trust formed at the outset can attract help from beyond the original circle.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-03
translation.text: Joining with others from a genuine inner commitment prevents self-betrayal. The relationship is sound because it begins in sincerity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-04
translation.text: Associating with the wrong people is a painful mistake. Companionship without judgment can injure rather than support a person.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-05
translation.text: Openly aligning with the worthy outside oneself means following what is higher and better. Loyalty should attach to virtue, not mere familiarity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-06
translation.text: Visible alliance is fortunate because the ruler’s position is centered and correct. In the hunting image, what resists is released while what comes willingly is accepted; subjects feel no need for alarm.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-08-07
translation.text: Association without a beginning or head cannot reach a proper conclusion. A community lacking a coherent basis has little prospect of lasting.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-01
translation.text: Wind passes high across the sky, indicating a small gathering of strength. The exemplary person cultivates grace in conduct and refinement in character.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-02
translation.text: Returning to one’s own right path is fortunate. The movement succeeds because it accords with what ought to be done.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-03
translation.text: Being drawn back toward the right course still preserves the center. Joining others in correction need not mean losing independent judgment.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-04
translation.text: The husband and wife turn against each other because the household relationship is not properly ordered. A damaged vehicle mirrors this internal discord.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-05
translation.text: Sincerity helps fear and danger recede because the yielding line shares the purpose of those above. Trust gives cooperation practical force.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-06
translation.text: Being bound together in good faith means not enjoying wealth alone. Prosperity has greater value when neighbors can share in it.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-09-07
translation.text: Rain has finally fallen because virtue and resources have accumulated. Yet further advance is suspect: completion calls for caution, not a new reckless campaign.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-01
translation.text: Heaven stands above and the lake below, each in its proper place. The exemplary person clarifies roles and distinctions so that people understand their responsibilities.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-02
translation.text: Walking simply on one’s own path fulfills a personal resolve. A modest start needs no borrowed grandeur.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-03
translation.text: The secluded person stays fortunate because inner balance is not upset by outside demands. A tranquil path arises from steadiness of mind.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-04
translation.text: Weak vision cannot supply clarity, and impaired walking cannot keep pace. The tiger’s bite follows an unsuitable position; the warrior’s ambition is strong but unwise.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-05
translation.text: Fearful caution while treading near the tiger brings a good ending. Such restraint enables the person’s intention to be fulfilled.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-06
translation.text: Decisive walking remains dangerous even in a proper position. Rank and authority do not cancel the need to consider the consequences of firmness.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-10-07
translation.text: Great fortune at the top signifies a cause for widespread celebration. Looking back over one’s conduct allows a fitting completion.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-01
translation.text: Heaven and Earth exchange their influences, producing peace and growth. The ruler supports this process by helping nature’s work and ensuring that people benefit from it.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-02
translation.text: Pulling up grass brings its roots and companion shoots. Going forward together is fortunate because the group’s intention reaches beyond itself.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-03
translation.text: Broad-minded conduct accords with the middle way and makes virtue shine more widely. Inclusion must be joined to fairness.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-04
translation.text: Nothing moves outward without eventually returning. Rise and decline belong to the changing boundary between Heaven and Earth.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-05
translation.text: Neighbors descend lightly without relying on wealth. Their trust reflects a heartfelt desire for fellowship rather than a calculated bargain.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-06
translation.text: The marriage alliance brings exceptional fortune because a centered intention can be carried out. Proper relationships translate purpose into action.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-11-07
translation.text: When a wall collapses back into the moat, government commands have become confused. The image warns that established order can break apart.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-01
translation.text: Heaven and Earth fail to communicate, illustrating stagnation. The exemplary person reduces outward display, preserves integrity, and refuses honors that would expose him to danger.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-02
translation.text: The grass and its roots hold together in upright resolve. Even during obstruction, the intention remains directed toward a worthy ruler.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-03
translation.text: A great person bears stagnation without mingling indiscriminately with the crowd. Keeping principle intact matters more than fitting in.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-04
translation.text: Concealed shame results from occupying an unsuitable position. A compromised role can force a person to hide what ought to be corrected.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-05
translation.text: Acting under a legitimate mandate is free from blame and allows the underlying purpose to advance.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-06
translation.text: The great person’s favorable outcome comes from occupying the correct position. Authority must remain aligned with responsibility.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-12-07
translation.text: Stagnation eventually overturns; it cannot last forever. A blocked situation contains the possibility of its own reversal.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-01
translation.text: Heaven and fire rise together in the image of fellowship. The exemplary person groups people and things by kind while recognizing the distinctions between them.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-02
translation.text: Going beyond the gate to join with others gives no cause for reproach. Genuine fellowship should not be limited to one household.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-03
translation.text: Associating only with one’s own clan is regrettable. Such narrow loyalty restricts the possibility of wider cooperation.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-04
translation.text: Troops hidden in brushwood confront a strong opponent. Their failure to move for three years reveals the danger and difficulty of that opposition.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-05
translation.text: Climbing the wall but refraining from attack means accepting that assault is not justified. Restraint allows the person to return to the appropriate rule.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-06
translation.text: The early tears of the allied people reflect honest inner purpose. After overcoming opposition, the armies can finally meet.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-13-07
translation.text: Fellowship on the outskirts carries no regret, but the larger aspiration remains unrealized. Peaceful contact is not yet complete unity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-01
translation.text: Fire shines high in Heaven, indicating great possession. The exemplary person restrains harmful conduct, promotes goodness, and honors Heaven’s favorable charge.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-02
translation.text: At the beginning of great possession, harmful association has not yet formed. Keeping clear of corrupt influence preserves one’s advantage.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-03
translation.text: A large wagon can carry heavy stores because its load is held securely at the center. Resources require dependable support.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-04
translation.text: A duke’s offering to the Son of Heaven entails responsibilities a petty person cannot bear. High honors without suitable character bring harm.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-05
translation.text: Refraining from ostentation avoids blame because the person sees the situation clearly. Knowing what not to display is a form of discernment.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-06
translation.text: Authentic trust inspires purpose, while appropriate dignity prevents complacency. Authority can remain accessible without surrendering necessary care.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-14-07
translation.text: Great good fortune at the summit is described as help from Heaven. The blessing is associated with worthy conduct rather than mere accumulation.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-01
translation.text: A mountain rests within Earth, a picture of modesty. The exemplary person reduces what is excessive and adds to what is lacking, distributing things fairly.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-02
translation.text: The deeply modest person governs the self through humility. Self-respect does not require superiority over others.
