translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-03
translation.text: Expressed modesty is fortunate because it comes from the heart. Genuine humility is an inward attainment, not a performance.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-04
translation.text: A worker who remains modest despite achievement gains the trust of the people. Earned authority has no need of boasting.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-05
translation.text: Actively showing modesty is favorable because it does not violate proper rules. Courtesy and effectiveness can coexist.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-06
translation.text: The expedition is directed against those who refuse proper order. In its ancient political setting, humility does not mean surrendering responsibility.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-15-07
translation.text: Although modest conduct is well known, the aspiration is still not wholly achieved. The permitted military action concerns restoring order in one’s own territory.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-01
translation.text: Thunder breaks forth from Earth, creating an image of joyful movement. Ancient kings established music to honor virtue and offered solemn sacrifices to Heaven and the ancestors.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-02
translation.text: Voicing delight too proudly leads to misfortune when ambition has reached its limit. Satisfaction should not become self-glorification.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-03
translation.text: Not waiting even a whole day to distinguish what is right is fortunate. Clear judgment comes from an inwardly centered and upright position.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-04
translation.text: Looking upward in restless pursuit of pleasure produces regret because the position is unsuitable. Approval-seeking disturbs good judgment.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-05
translation.text: The great gathering around a source of enthusiasm allows a far-reaching purpose to be realized. Trust turns common joy into collective achievement.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-06
translation.text: Persistent illness in the fifth line comes from resting above a firm line. The central position nevertheless prevents total collapse.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-16-07
translation.text: Blind delight at the top cannot endure. Enjoyment disconnected from judgment eventually becomes exhausted.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-01
translation.text: Thunder rests within the lake. The exemplary person follows the rhythm of the day, withdrawing at dusk to rest rather than forcing continuous activity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-02
translation.text: A change of office is favorable if it follows what is right. Going outside to form relationships can produce results without compromising one’s principles.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-03
translation.text: Binding oneself to the child excludes the grown man. Not every competing attachment can be maintained at the same time.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-04
translation.text: Following the mature person means leaving the lesser attachment behind. The direction of one’s loyalty shapes what is possible.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-05
translation.text: Gaining followers can be dangerous when acquisition becomes an end in itself. Sincere adherence to the way makes the purpose clear.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-06
translation.text: Trust placed in what is excellent is fortunate because the position is right and central. The quality of what one follows matters.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-17-07
translation.text: Binding and tying someone at the very top shows that the situation has gone too far. Forced attachment cannot continue without limit.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-01
translation.text: Wind moves beneath a mountain, stirring up what has decayed. The exemplary person awakens the community and cultivates character in order to correct entrenched faults.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-02
translation.text: Repairing the father’s mistakes is ultimately an act of honoring the parent. Responsible succession includes correcting inherited damage.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-03
translation.text: Remedying the mother’s errors calls for a balanced approach. Harsh insistence would violate the proper middle way.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-04
translation.text: Working to repair the father’s mistakes may bring small regrets, but the conclusion need not involve serious blame.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-05
translation.text: Indulging the father’s faults fails to accomplish the needed change. Continued delay carries regret.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-06
translation.text: Correcting inherited mistakes with integrity earns respect. Honor arises when the successor carries forward what is worthy.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-18-07
translation.text: Not serving kings and nobles can express an example-worthy resolve. Independence may preserve a moral purpose beyond office.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-01
translation.text: Earth lies above the lake, portraying attentive approach. The exemplary person teaches tirelessly and protects the people with enduring generosity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-02
translation.text: Approaching others through sympathetic understanding is fortunate because the purpose advances in a right direction.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-03
translation.text: The second sympathetic approach is favorable, yet does not simply submit to command. Genuine responsiveness retains independent judgment.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-04
translation.text: Sweet words without substance arise from an unsuitable position. Recognizing this failing and becoming concerned can keep the error from lasting.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-05
translation.text: Arriving with full attention brings no blame because the position fits the task. Presence must be matched by appropriate conduct.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-06
translation.text: A wise ruler acts through the middle way. Sound oversight is neither neglectful nor excessively controlling.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-19-07
translation.text: Generous and substantial approach is fortunate because the intention comes from within. Care for others must be deeply rooted.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-01
translation.text: Wind travels across Earth, making conditions visible. Early kings inspected different regions and then adapted their instruction to the people they observed.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-02
translation.text: A childlike way of looking sees little beyond appearances. For an ordinary person that may be understandable, but a responsible leader should know better.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-03
translation.text: Looking through a narrow opening is a limited viewpoint. The commentary criticizes such restricted observation in the language of its own age.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-04
translation.text: Examining one’s own life helps determine whether to advance or withdraw. Thoughtful self-observation keeps a person from losing the way.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-05
translation.text: Observing the splendor of a state suggests honorable service as the ruler’s guest. Recognition must reflect genuine merit.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-06
translation.text: A ruler who examines personal conduct should also observe the condition of the people. The public response reveals the effects of government.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-20-07
translation.text: Looking at the lives of others still requires an unsettled conscience. Even from a higher position, vigilance and reflection remain necessary.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-01
translation.text: Thunder and lightning accompany each other, the image of biting through obstruction. Ancient rulers made penalties clear and established enforceable laws.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-02
translation.text: Stocks that cover the toes keep a wrongdoer from continuing. Early correction can stop a harmful course before it grows.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-03
translation.text: Biting through soft flesh until the nose sinks in indicates force applied close at hand. The yielding line acts above a firm one.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-04
translation.text: Encountering poison results from being in the wrong place. The difficulty of enforcing order can arise from the enforcer’s own position.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-05
translation.text: Perseverance through difficulty is fortunate, although the work has not yet reached full clarity. Punishment alone is not complete justice.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-06
translation.text: Careful constancy amid danger avoids blame because the action fits its circumstances. The right measure is crucial.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-21-07
translation.text: A heavy collar covering the ears shows a failure to listen and understand. Severe punishment follows persistent moral deafness.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-01
translation.text: Fire brightens the mountain’s foot, suggesting ornament and illumination. The exemplary person clarifies routine public affairs but does not hastily decide major criminal cases.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-02
translation.text: Leaving the carriage and walking is a deliberate rejection of an improper privilege. A choice can be dignified precisely because it is modest.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-03
translation.text: Adorning the beard depends on what stands above it. Ornament is secondary to the person or substance that it embellishes.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-04
translation.text: Long-lasting correctness brings good fortune because no one can ultimately diminish it. True beauty rests on integrity.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-05
translation.text: The fourth line’s uncertainty comes from its position. What seemed threatening turns out to be a marriage proposal, and the matter ends without reproach.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-06
translation.text: The fifth line’s good fortune brings joy. Simple gifts offered sincerely can be more fitting than lavish display.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-22-07
translation.text: Plain white ornament avoids blame because aspiration at the top has found its proper expression. Simplicity completes refinement.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-01
translation.text: A mountain rises upon Earth, yet its base must remain secure. Those in authority should strengthen and support the people below so that homes remain safe.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-02
translation.text: The bed begins to be stripped at its feet. Weakening the foundation destroys what supports everything above.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-03
translation.text: As the bed is stripped further, no effective allies remain. Deterioration spreads when no one can provide support.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-04
translation.text: One can separate from the forces of disintegration without blame. This departure cuts ties with what is failing above and below.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-05
translation.text: The damage has reached the skin, making disaster immediate. What began beneath the surface can no longer be ignored.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-06
translation.text: Orderly favor shown to the palace women brings no final reproach. Proper arrangement can limit conflict during an unstable time.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-23-07
translation.text: The exemplary person receives a carriage because the people support him; the petty person loses even his shelter. The contrast concerns the consequences of conduct.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-01
translation.text: Thunder lies hidden in Earth, indicating the beginning of a return. At the turning of the season, ancient kings closed the passes and allowed people and rulers to rest.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-02
translation.text: Returning before one has strayed far permits moral self-cultivation. Small errors are easier to repair when recognized early.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-03
translation.text: The auspicious return is accompanied by a humble concern for others. Renewed goodness is strengthened through benevolence.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-04
translation.text: Repeatedly turning back can be perilous, but the intention to correct oneself is not blameworthy. Recovery may require several attempts.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-05
translation.text: Walking among others, one person returns alone because of commitment to the right path. Conscience may require independent action.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-06
translation.text: A substantial return leaves no regret because the person examines the self from a centered standpoint.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-24-07
translation.text: Being lost and unable to return is disastrous because it opposes the way a ruler should follow. Persistent error eventually affects the whole community.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-01
translation.text: Thunder moves beneath Heaven, and all things proceed without falsity. Ancient rulers responded attentively to the season and nourished living beings.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-02
translation.text: Going forward without delusion allows an honest purpose to be fulfilled. Right action begins without contrivance.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-03
translation.text: Not farming solely for the harvest shows freedom from a calculating expectation of wealth. Work should follow what is appropriate, not only immediate gain.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-04
translation.text: The passerby gets the cow, but the townspeople suffer the loss. Misfortune may fall on those who did not cause the event.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-05
translation.text: Firmly preserving what is right brings no blame. Constancy matters especially when the circumstances are uncertain.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-06
translation.text: The illness that occurs without wrongdoing should not prompt indiscriminate remedies. In this textual setting the warning is against needless intervention, not modern medical care.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-25-07
translation.text: Acting without delusion can still bring misfortune when the course has reached its limit. Good intentions cannot erase the demands of timing.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-01
translation.text: Heaven appears enclosed within a mountain, the image of great accumulation. The exemplary person studies the words and deeds of earlier generations to deepen personal character.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-02
translation.text: When danger lies ahead, stopping is beneficial. Restraint keeps one from entering an avoidable disaster.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-03
translation.text: The carriage loses its axle fitting, yet inner balance keeps this from becoming a moral fault. Temporary immobility may be necessary.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-04
translation.text: Going forward becomes advantageous when the intention agrees with those above. Preparation and disciplined strength make advancement fitting.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-05
translation.text: The fourth line brings great fortune and joy. Restraining harmful power while it is young prevents later injury.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-06
translation.text: The fifth line’s good fortune is a cause for celebration. Managing the source of danger is wiser than fighting its symptoms.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-26-07
translation.text: The open road across Heaven indicates that the way can now be widely carried out. What was restrained has found constructive release.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-01
translation.text: Thunder stirs beneath the mountain, creating the image of nourishment. The exemplary person watches speech carefully and practices moderation in food and drink.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-02
translation.text: Staring at another person’s food after abandoning one’s own resources is hardly admirable. Desire can undermine self-sufficiency.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-03
translation.text: The second line’s journey is unfortunate because it departs from its proper company. Seeking support in the wrong place creates dependence.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-04
translation.text: Being unable to nourish oneself properly for ten years shows a profound departure from the right way. The problem is structural, not momentary.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-05
translation.text: The fourth line’s reversed search for nourishment is fortunate because help from above can be shared openly. The higher position extends its benefits.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-06
translation.text: The fifth line is fortunate in staying steady and following a suitable guide. Dependence can be appropriate when exercised with humility.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-27-07
translation.text: Nourishment originating from the top may be dangerous but fortunate, and it brings broad blessing. Great responsibility accompanies the ability to sustain others.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-01
translation.text: The lake rises above the trees and overwhelms them. The exemplary person stands independently without fear, and can withdraw from public life without resentment.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-02
translation.text: Using white reeds as a mat expresses care and gentleness at the foundation. Deliberate preparation reduces the chance of harm.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-03
translation.text: An old man marrying a young woman is presented as an unusual pairing. The commentary highlights a relationship that crosses an ordinary boundary.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-04
translation.text: A sagging roof beam spells danger because nothing adequately supports it. A structure cannot survive indefinitely without reinforcement.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-05
translation.text: The raised, firm beam is fortunate because it no longer bends beneath the load. Sound support makes strength useful.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-06
translation.text: Flowers on an old poplar cannot last; likewise the pairing of an older woman and younger man is treated as irregular in the ancient text. Brief flourishing is not the same as enduring renewal.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-28-07
translation.text: Crossing water so deeply that it covers the head is dangerous, yet the deed is not necessarily blameworthy. The commentary distinguishes harmful outcomes from culpable intentions.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-01
translation.text: Water follows water in successive depths, an image of repeated danger. The exemplary person keeps conduct steady and rehearses teaching and public duties.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-02
translation.text: Falling deeper into the pit is disastrous because the right path has been lost. Repeated exposure to danger does not make an error harmless.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-03
translation.text: Only a small gain is possible because the person has not yet escaped the middle of the danger. Ambition must be scaled to reality.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-04
translation.text: Moving from one pit to another accomplishes nothing in the end. Action without a safe route only multiplies exposure.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-05
translation.text: The simple offering of wine and food works through cooperation between firmness and gentleness. Sincerity can matter more than display.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-06
translation.text: The pit is not yet full because the central position has not reached its full measure. Relief is partial and restraint remains necessary.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-29-07
translation.text: The final line spends three years in danger because the proper way has been lost. Prolonged confinement is the result of failing to correct course.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-01
translation.text: Light shines twice, the image of repeated fire. A great person carries illumination onward so that its beneficial influence reaches the four directions.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-02
translation.text: Carefulness amid confused steps prevents blame. Respectful attention is essential when clarity is not yet established.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-03
translation.text: Yellow light brings great good fortune because it occupies the central path. Balanced brightness is more reliable than dazzling display.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-04
translation.text: The setting sun cannot remain at its height. The commentary points to the inevitable limits of a passing stage.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-05
translation.text: A sudden flare cannot find a lasting place. A force that appears violently may disappear just as quickly.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-06
translation.text: The fifth line’s good fortune is linked to the ruler’s position. Grief and vigilance can accompany responsible authority.

translation.title: Image Commentary I / XIANG-U XIANG-U-30-07
translation.text: The ruler’s expedition seeks to rectify the state. The proper purpose of coercive force, in this classical account, is to restore just order.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-01
translation.text: A lake rests upon a mountain: this is Influence. The exemplary person welcomes others with an open and receptive mind.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-02
translation.text: The stirring of the big toe shows that the intention is already directed outward, although movement has barely begun.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-03
translation.text: Remaining still is fortunate even amid danger, because yielding appropriately avoids harm.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-04
translation.text: Feeling the influence in the thighs prevents remaining still; merely following others reveals a low and dependent purpose.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-05
translation.text: Steadfastness removes regret because influence has not brought harm. Restless thoughts, however, cannot accomplish something broad.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-06
translation.text: Influence felt in the back shows that the aspiration has reached only an outer or limited part of the person.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-31-07
translation.text: Influence confined to jaw, cheeks, and tongue is little more than persuasive speech, not deep or lasting feeling.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-01
translation.text: Thunder and wind operate together in Constancy. The exemplary person establishes a firm direction and does not casually abandon it.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-02
translation.text: Seeking excessive depth or permanence from the outset invites misfortune; durability must develop over time.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-03
translation.text: The second line loses regret because it can sustain a balanced course for a long time.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-04
translation.text: When a person cannot maintain virtue consistently, there is no secure place for that person to be accepted.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-05
translation.text: Remaining a long time in an unsuitable position cannot produce the game sought in the hunt.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-06
translation.text: The text praises a wife's constancy within ancient marital roles, while warning that a husband must judge duty himself; this reflects historical role expectations.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-32-07
translation.text: Agitated persistence at the highest place achieves little. Restlessness is the opposite of genuine constancy.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-01
translation.text: A mountain stands beneath Heaven, depicting Retreat. The exemplary person keeps distance from unworthy influences without hatred, while maintaining dignity.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-02
translation.text: Retreating last is dangerous; if one refrains from going forward, the danger need not arise.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-03
translation.text: The yellow oxhide signifies a determination bound so firmly that it cannot easily be loosened.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-04
translation.text: Retreat entangled by attachments brings weakness and distress. Managing minor household affairs is possible, but great undertakings are inappropriate.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-05
translation.text: An exemplary person can choose a graceful retreat, whereas a petty person finds such withdrawal difficult.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-06
translation.text: Timely and worthy retreat is fortunate because it sets the intention right.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-33-07
translation.text: A generous and unencumbered retreat encounters no disadvantage because nothing remains to cause doubt.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-34-01
translation.text: Thunder resounds in Heaven in Great Strength. The exemplary person refuses to take any step contrary to proper conduct.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-34-02
translation.text: Strength expressed only in the toes soon reaches its limit. Bold movement without judgment cannot last.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-34-03
translation.text: The second line is fortunate through constancy because it occupies a balanced position.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-34-04
translation.text: A petty person uses brute strength; the exemplary person declines to act that way.

translation.text: The fence breaks and the ram's horns are freed; obstacles have opened, making continued advancement possible.

translation.text: Losing the ram results from occupying an unsuitable position, not simply from a shortage of force.

translation.text: Light rises above Earth in Progress. The exemplary person makes personal virtue increasingly bright and visible.

translation.text: Progress initially meets resistance, yet upright solitary conduct remains valid. Being patient before receiving a mandate avoids blame.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-35-03
translation.text: Great blessings come through occupying a central and correct position.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-35-04

translation.text: The grasping field mouse faces danger because its position is unsuitable.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-35-06
translation.text: Do not become consumed by gains or losses: proceeding with purpose can bring celebration.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-35-07
translation.text: Using strength only to discipline one's own city shows that the larger way has not yet shone fully.

translation.text: The traveler goes without food because loyalty to what is right outweighs personal comfort.

translation.text: The second line is fortunate because its responsiveness follows appropriate standards.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-36-04
translation.text: The aim of the southern hunt is fulfilled when the principal source of harm is found.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-36-05
translation.text: Entering the left side signifies gaining insight into the concealed intentions of the threatening power.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-36-06
translation.text: Jizi's constancy shows that inner light must not be extinguished even when outward circumstances are dark.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-36-07
translation.text: At first the light rose and illuminated the four regions; later it fell into darkness through loss of proper measure.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-01
translation.text: Wind issues from fire in The Family. The exemplary person speaks with substance and acts consistently.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-02
translation.text: Establishing household boundaries early prevents regret while intentions have not yet shifted.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-03
translation.text: The second line's good fortune comes from receptive and accommodating conduct.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-04
translation.text: Firm household discipline is not necessarily mistaken; excessive joking without boundaries disrupts family order.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-05
translation.text: The prosperity of the household is fortunate because each person fulfills an appropriate position.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-06
translation.text: The ruler reaching the family shows reciprocal affection and mutual care.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-37-07
translation.text: Dignity brings good fortune when it begins with examining and correcting oneself.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-01
translation.text: Fire rises while the lake lies below: Opposition. The exemplary person recognizes shared ground without erasing real differences.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-02
translation.text: Encountering a disagreeable person may prevent greater blame when handled with caution.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-03
translation.text: Meeting the master in a narrow lane does not mean the right course has been lost.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-04

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-05
translation.text: Mutual trust overcomes estrangement and makes the purpose attainable.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-06
translation.text: Reunion with one's own kin allows forward movement to bring good fortune.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-38-07
translation.text: Rain dissolves the accumulated suspicions; what seemed hostile can become a fortunate meeting.

translation.text: Water stands above a mountain in Obstruction. The exemplary person turns inward to examine conduct and cultivate virtue.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-39-02
translation.text: Forward movement encounters difficulty, while return earns respect. This is a time to wait.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-39-03
translation.text: A minister struggles repeatedly for the ruler rather than personal advantage, and ultimately deserves no reproach.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-39-04
translation.text: Returning from obstruction brings joy to those within one's circle.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-39-05
translation.text: Returning to join others after difficulty is suitable because the position is solid.

translation.text: During great obstruction, companions arrive when one maintains a measured center.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-39-07
translation.text: Returning instead of forcing the road yields substance; seeking a worthy superior accords with the inward purpose.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-40-02
translation.text: At the meeting of firmness and gentleness, no blame arises when their relation is fitting.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-40-03
translation.text: The second line's perseverance is fortunate because it has reached the middle way.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-40-04
translation.text: Carrying a load while riding in privilege invites disgrace and attackers; one cannot blame others for risks produced by one's own behavior.

translation.text: Freeing the big toe indicates removal of a constraint, yet the present position is still not fully appropriate.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-40-06
translation.text: When the exemplary person achieves release, petty and obstructive influences withdraw.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-40-07

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-01

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-02
translation.text: Quickly assisting another after one's own duties are done brings the intention into accord with those above.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-03
translation.text: The second line favors constancy because balance has become the core intention.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-04
translation.text: When three travel together, suspicion may divide them; simpler companionship can allow trust to form.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-05
translation.text: Removing an illness or defect is cause for joy, for decrease can be healing rather than deprivation.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-06
translation.text: The fifth line's great fortune is described as help received from above.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-41-07
translation.text: Helping others without unnecessary self-diminishment allows a significant aspiration to be fulfilled.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-42-01
translation.text: Wind and thunder combine in Increase. On seeing goodness, the exemplary person adopts it; on finding an error, corrects it.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-42-02
translation.text: Great good fortune without blame reflects the need not to overload those in lower positions.

translation.text: Unexpected benefit arrives from outside, showing that increase is not always self-produced.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-42-04
translation.text: Providing support during calamity belongs to one's established responsibilities.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-42-05
translation.text: The duke accepts the report because it advances a beneficial purpose.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-42-06
translation.text: Sincere generosity need not be questioned; receiving goodwill in return greatly fulfills one's intention.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-42-07

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-43-02
translation.text: Advancing without being able to win produces blame; determination must be joined to capacity.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-43-03
translation.text: Even with soldiers appearing at night, a centered stance prevents panic.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-43-04
translation.text: The exemplary person's firm resolve ultimately avoids blame when it serves what is right.

translation.text: Hesitant walking reflects an unsuitable position; refusing advice shows a failure to hear clearly.

translation.text: Walking the middle way avoids blame, although the central intention has not yet become fully bright.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-44-03
translation.text: Having a fish in the wrapper is not meant to extend to the guest; possession carries limits of proper use.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-44-04
translation.text: Difficult walking persists, but the person's progress has not been drawn into a binding entanglement.

translation.text: The misfortune of having no fish reflects estrangement from the people.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-45-03

translation.text: Proceeding without blame is possible through accommodating those above.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-45-07
translation.text: Tears and lament express insecurity in relation to those above, not merely private sadness.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-46-04

translation.text: Petty preoccupation during travel brings disaster when aspirations have reached a dead end.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-56-03
translation.text: A loyal young attendant ultimately brings no reproach to the wanderer.

translation.text: Indecision reveals a doubtful purpose; disciplined firmness restores direction.

translation.text: Wind moves across water in Dispersion. Earlier kings offered sacrifice to Heaven and established ancestral temples to renew a shared center.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-59-02
translation.text: The first line's rescue is fortunate because it responds promptly and cooperatively.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-59-03
translation.text: Running to the support of the table brings fulfillment of a deeply held wish.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-59-04
translation.text: Dispersing personal attachments directs one's purpose beyond private self-interest.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-59-05
translation.text: Dispersing a narrow faction brings great good fortune because a wider common purpose becomes possible.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-59-06
translation.text: The ruler's residence is without blame when authority occupies its proper place.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-59-07
translation.text: Dispersing bloodshed and fleeing danger keeps harm at a distance.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-01
translation.text: Water rests above a lake in Limitation. The exemplary person sets measures and standards and deliberates about virtuous conduct.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-02
translation.text: Remaining inside the courtyard avoids blame because one understands when passage is open and when it is blocked.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-03
translation.text: Refusing to leave even the gate becomes unfortunate when the crucial opportunity has been missed.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-04
translation.text: The person who refuses all restraint has cause to lament; that failing cannot simply be blamed on others.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-05
translation.text: Peaceful limitation prospers because it follows a worthy higher principle.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-06
translation.text: Sweet and fitting restraint is fortunate because it occupies a balanced position.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-60-07
translation.text: Harsh restriction pursued without change reaches a dead end; bitter limits cannot endure.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-01
translation.text: Wind moves over the lake in Inner Truth. The exemplary person deliberates carefully in legal matters and delays irreversible death sentences.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-02
translation.text: Prudent preparation is fortunate because the initial intention has not been changed.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-03
translation.text: A young crane echoes its parent because the response arises sincerely from within.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-04
translation.text: Indecisive drumming or silence reflects an unsuitable position and wavering confidence.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-05
translation.text: Losing the paired horses symbolizes leaving one's own circle to turn toward a higher commitment.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-06
translation.text: Trust binds people together without blame because the position is correct.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-61-07
translation.text: The rooster's call cannot truly rise to Heaven; boastful sound without matching substance cannot last.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-01
translation.text: Thunder rises above a mountain in Small Exceeding. The exemplary person leans toward added respect, sincere mourning, and economical daily use.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-02
translation.text: A bird flying too high meets disaster that can no longer readily be prevented.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-03
translation.text: Stopping short of the ruler and meeting the minister observes a boundary that subjects should not overstep.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-04
translation.text: Careless following leaves a person exposed to violence; the danger can be severe.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-05
translation.text: A suitable meeting avoids blame, but going forward is perilous; continued vigilance is needed because the condition cannot last.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-06
translation.text: Dense clouds fail to produce rain because the force has risen too high.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-62-07
translation.text: Passing beyond the proper meeting point is excessive ascent, inviting the bird's misfortune.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-01
translation.text: Water stands above fire in After Completion. The exemplary person anticipates future trouble and prepares before it arrives.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-02
translation.text: Holding back the wheels is right and causes no blame; early caution protects what is already achieved.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-03
translation.text: What is lost returns after seven days because patience follows a balanced course.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-04
translation.text: Three years of campaigning bring victory, but the long struggle has exhausted those involved.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-05
translation.text: Remaining alert throughout the day reflects awareness of possible dangers beneath apparent success.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-06
translation.text: The eastern neighbor's lavish ox sacrifice is less timely than the western neighbor's modest rite; true blessing follows appropriate timing.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-63-07
translation.text: When the head is immersed, danger is immediate; that degree of overreach cannot continue.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-01
translation.text: Fire rests above water in Before Completion. The exemplary person carefully distinguishes things and assigns each its appropriate place.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-02
translation.text: Wetting the tail shows failure to recognize the limit of what can safely be attempted.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-03
translation.text: The second line is fortunate because moderation guides action along the correct course.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-04
translation.text: Advancing before completion is dangerous because the present position does not fit the task.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-05
translation.text: Steadfastness ends regret, allowing the underlying aspiration to be carried out.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-06
translation.text: The exemplary person's light spreads brightness and brings good fortune to others.

translation.title: Image Commentary II / XIANG-L XIANG-L-64-07
translation.text: Drinking until the head is soaked reveals a failure to recognize moderation and proper limits.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-01
translation.text: Yuan is the beginning and leading force of goodness; heng is the gathering of favorable conditions; li is the harmony between benefit and what is right; and zhen is the firm foundation on which affairs can be completed. A cultivated person embodies compassion in leading others, brings people together in a manner consistent with proper conduct, benefits things without violating justice, and remains steadfast when carrying out responsibilities. These are not four promises of effortless success. They describe four qualities that make constructive action possible. The Qian hexagram is therefore characterized by yuan, heng, li, and zhen.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-02
translation.text: The hidden dragon represents someone with exceptional character who has not yet stepped into public view. Such a person does not change convictions simply to follow fashion or rush to secure recognition. Living apart from public affairs need not cause resentment, and being overlooked need not lead to bitterness. One acts when doing so accords with one's principles and refrains when the circumstances are troubling. The decisive quality is an inner resolve that cannot easily be uprooted. The image of the concealed dragon thus presents restraint as a positive expression of strength, not as evidence of weakness.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-03
translation.text: The dragon appearing in the field describes a person of sound character whose influence is beginning to become visible. Trustworthiness should be evident in everyday speech, care in ordinary actions, and sincerity in resisting dishonest impulses. A person can contribute to the welfare of society without boasting of those contributions. When conduct is consistently good, its influence can spread beyond the individual. The commentary calls this the virtue appropriate to a ruler: moral authority begins with how someone behaves in unremarkable situations, well before power and public reputation become prominent.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-04
translation.text: The third line portrays a conscientious person working diligently throughout the day and remaining watchful at night. The explanation links this vigilance to the cultivation of character and the responsible pursuit of work. Loyalty and trust develop virtue, while thoughtful language and sincerity help sustain meaningful undertakings. One should recognize the early signs of an opportunity and know when to advance, but also recognize when an undertaking has reached its proper end. Neither holding a higher position nor occupying a lower one should produce arrogance or despair. Attentiveness to changing circumstances makes it possible to navigate danger without incurring blame.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-05
translation.text: The dragon that may leap but still remains near the depths illustrates a period of uncertain transition. Moving up or down does not by itself indicate dishonesty, and changing between advance and withdrawal does not necessarily mean abandoning one's companions. A thoughtful person continues to develop abilities and character while waiting for a fitting opportunity. The essential point is to distinguish flexibility from opportunism. An action may be right at one moment and premature at another. Because the person responds to the time rather than forcing a fixed course, the text says that blame can be avoided.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-06
translation.text: When the dragon flies in the sky, its influence is fully visible. The commentary explains this by observing that similar sounds answer one another and similar energies seek each other out. Water flows toward damp ground, fire takes readily to dry material, clouds accompany the dragon, and wind accompanies the tiger. In the same way, when a sage emerges, others perceive and respond to that person's influence. Beings associated with heaven tend upward, while those associated with earth tend downward. The image emphasizes resonance and natural affinity rather than the idea that public authority can be established through force alone.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-07
translation.text: The dragon that climbs too high reaches a precarious condition. Someone may appear distinguished yet lack a secure and legitimate position, stand above others without their support, or be surrounded by capable people who are unable or unwilling to help. Height and prestige are therefore not sufficient measures of sound leadership. Once a person becomes isolated from both ordinary people and trustworthy advisers, taking further action can bring regret. The warning concerns overextension: a position that looks impressive may already have lost the relationships and foundations needed to sustain it.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-08
translation.text: The expression 'Hidden dragon; do not act' indicates a condition of being below or out of public sight. This does not condemn the person's abilities. It says that those abilities have not yet reached the stage at which they can be exercised openly. The location of the first line helps explain the restraint called for in the original judgment. Recognizing a low or preliminary position is part of recognizing the correct time for action. The emphasis is on patient preparation, not permanent withdrawal.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-09
translation.text: 'The dragon appears in the field' marks a time when valuable character can begin to be recognized. The phrase 'the time allows it to remain' suggests that the emerging individual has found a place where talents may be displayed without rushing beyond the circumstances. Unlike the hidden dragon, this stage permits contact with others and the beginnings of public influence. Yet the position is still one of development rather than complete authority. The lesson lies in accepting the opportunities available at this particular stage.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-10
translation.text: 'Diligent throughout the day' points to someone actively engaged in responsibilities. The language is not merely a compliment about being busy. It places continued effort within a phase when decisions and conduct can have consequences. Work requires attention, persistence, and an awareness that one's position is changing. The accompanying warning about vigilance is therefore meaningful: activity should be sustained by reflection rather than performed mechanically. The line describes an active stage of cultivation and practical engagement.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-11
translation.text: 'Perhaps leaping, yet remaining in the depths' describes a person testing whether the time is right to rise. The commentary's brief explanation, 'testing oneself,' emphasizes uncertainty rather than failure. Abilities may be ready, but circumstances still need to be assessed. A trial movement may reveal whether advancement is appropriate, and hesitation may prevent a premature commitment. The image captures the point between private preparation and full public action, when judgment matters as much as courage.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-12
translation.text: 'The dragon flies in the sky' signifies effective governance from a higher position. The commentary shifts attention from the mere image of height to its public consequences: someone who has reached the appropriate level can now exercise responsibility. Visibility must be matched by the capacity to bring order and benefit to others. The image is therefore not simply about promotion or personal success. It concerns the stage at which developed virtue and ability are placed where they can shape collective affairs.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-13
translation.text: 'The overreaching dragon has regret' warns of the distress that follows when development passes its sustainable limit. The phrase 'the calamity of exhaustion' describes a situation in which further progress is no longer possible on the same terms. A person who has reached the extreme may mistake height for permanence and overlook the signs of decline. The statement offers a compact explanation of the warning in the top line: without an awareness of limits, apparent achievement can turn into misfortune.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-14
translation.text: 'Qian's use of the nines' is explained as a condition in which the world is well ordered. Unlike the image of a solitary ruler standing above the rest, this statement points to the coordinated operation of strong forces. Its brevity should not obscure the distinction: the mature use of strength is not endless competition to become first. It is the proper arrangement of capacities so that order becomes possible. The passage interprets the special 'use of nine' statement in terms of governance rather than individual display.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-15
translation.text: 'Hidden dragon; do not act' is here explained through the language of energy: the yang force remains concealed. The commentary describes the natural condition of an emerging power before it has become manifest. Something can exist and be developing even when it cannot yet be seen. The first stage of Qian is thus a time for conserving and forming strength. Bringing it prematurely into the open would ignore the relationship between development and timing. Concealment is part of the process, not necessarily an obstacle to it.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-16
translation.text: 'The dragon appears in the field' is associated here with the world becoming illuminated and civilized. The commentary broadens the earlier account of personal virtue into a social image: when constructive abilities come into view, they can begin to influence the surrounding world. The dragon's appearance does not mean the process is complete. Rather, it marks the emergence of a force whose effects may now be recognized. The emphasis falls on the public visibility of positive character and the gradual spread of its influence.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-17
translation.text: 'Diligent throughout the day' is interpreted as keeping pace with the time. Constant effort has value because it responds to developing circumstances rather than resisting change. A cultivated person must neither rest upon earlier achievements nor move blindly without observing what has altered. This stage calls for steady work, continual learning, and vigilance. To move with the time means bringing one's conduct into line with what the moment requires. The commentary thus connects diligence with adaptability.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-18
translation.text: 'Perhaps leaping, yet remaining in the depths' signifies a turning point in the Way of Qian. The image portrays neither settled withdrawal nor secure ascendance. It is the moment when an established pattern begins to change and a different level of action becomes possible. Because the transformation has not yet been completed, certainty would be misplaced. The commentary encourages awareness of the transition itself: when the underlying conditions shift, the way strength is expressed must also change.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-19
translation.text: 'The dragon flies in the sky' means that a person has reached a position from which heavenly virtue can be expressed. The focus is not on height alone. The appropriate position enables a cultivated individual to put the qualities of Qian into practice in a visible and consequential manner. Strength, sound judgment, and responsibility should now be apparent in conduct. This stage differs from the hidden or testing stages because capacity and opportunity have come together.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-20
translation.text: 'The overreaching dragon has regret' is linked to the time itself reaching an extreme. Even a successful development has a limit. When the circumstances that sustained an ascent have been exhausted, continuing to rise in the same manner becomes hazardous. The commentary treats excess as a temporal condition as well as a personal failing. Wise action requires noticing when a period is ending, rather than believing that its earlier momentum will continue indefinitely.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-21
translation.text: 'Qian's use of the nines' allows the pattern of heaven to be seen. The phrase points beyond any single dragon or individual achievement to the principles governing the whole process. Strength is expressed through change, timing, and the proper relation among different stages. Observing all the lines together makes that pattern clearer. The special statement therefore invites the reader to understand Qian as an ordered movement of forces rather than a command to dominate others.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-22
translation.text: The originating force of Qian allows things to begin and develop; benefit and steadfastness express the character and proper direction of that development. Qian bestows benefits widely without restricting them to a favored recipient. Its greatness rests on vigor, balance, rectitude, and purity. The six lines reveal different situations through which this force may unfold. The six dragons, moving with their proper times, symbolize the ordering of heavenly processes. Clouds travel, rain falls, and the world is brought into harmony. The passage presents creative strength as generative and widely beneficial, not as mere forcefulness.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-23
translation.text: A cultivated person's actions should make acquired virtue visible in daily life. Yet the image of hiding has a specific meaning: character may have developed privately without having reached a form ready for public expression. The work is not complete simply because the intention is good. In the first stage, withdrawal helps protect an unfinished undertaking. The text therefore distinguishes possessing potential from having the conditions and demonstrated practice needed to use it. Restraint can be faithful to the goal of mature action.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-24
translation.text: A cultivated person gathers understanding through study, clarifies it by asking questions, receives others with generosity, and puts it into action through benevolence. These four practices connect learning with ethical conduct. Knowledge alone is insufficient if it is not tested by inquiry and translated into how others are treated. The passage uses these qualities to explain the dragon appearing in the field: the virtues appropriate to leadership are already taking shape through education, openness, and practical care. Public influence should grow from that foundation.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-25
translation.text: The third line contains strong yang energy but does not occupy a central position. It stands above the field without yet reaching the domain of heaven. That unstable middle condition explains why the person must work energetically and remain alert. Neither status nor circumstances offer complete security. Vigilance does not mean panic; it means recognizing the particular risks of an intermediate stage. Even when danger exists, disciplined conduct can prevent blame. The passage reads the line's demanding language through its place in the six-line structure.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-26
translation.text: The fourth line is also strongly yang but not central. It is no longer situated in the field below, has not yet arrived at heaven above, and does not neatly occupy the ordinary human position between them. That uncertainty is why the line says 'perhaps.' The word signals an unresolved choice about advancing or remaining where one is. A cautious trial or pause is appropriate while the situation remains ambiguous. The commentary treats doubt as a feature of transition, and careful judgment as the way to avoid blame.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-27
translation.text: A great person brings conduct into accord with the virtue of heaven and earth, with the brightness of sun and moon, and with the succession of the seasons. Even the traditional language of spirits and good or bad fortune points to this comprehensive harmony. Acting ahead of an event does not violate the heavenly pattern, while acting afterward still observes the proper time. The passage describes an ideal of wisdom so thoroughly attuned to change that action is neither premature nor belated. Its claims belong to the philosophical and cosmological language of the text, rather than to a testable promise of prediction.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-01-28
translation.text: To be excessively high is to know only how to advance, not how to withdraw; to notice continued existence but forget the possibility of loss; and to value gain without preparing for deprivation. Such one-sided thinking creates the danger expressed by the overreaching dragon. The passage closes by praising the rare person who understands advance and retreat, survival and decline, gain and loss, while still preserving what is right. True wisdom is not unlimited expansion. It is the ability to recognize opposing possibilities and act without abandoning sound principles.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-01
translation.text: Kun is supremely yielding, yet its movement can be strong; it is supremely still, yet its character remains upright and firmly shaped. These qualities are not contradictions. Receptivity allows Kun to support the initiating activity represented by Qian and to carry things through to completion. By following the appropriate lead, it keeps to a reliable pattern, embraces the many forms of life, and enables them to flourish. Its distinctive power lies in receiving, nurturing, and acting at the proper time. The passage praises responsiveness as an active virtue rather than simple passivity.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-02
translation.text: A family that steadily accumulates good conduct may leave benefits to later generations, just as persistent wrongdoing can produce harm. The text illustrates this cumulative process with the grave examples of a minister killing his ruler and a son killing his father. Such events do not arise overnight; they are preceded by small developments that were not recognized or corrected early enough. 'Treading on frost; hard ice will come' summarizes this principle. The passage urges attention to early signs because repeated choices can gradually establish a direction that becomes difficult to reverse.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-03
translation.text: Straightness refers to inner rectitude, while squareness describes outward conduct shaped by what is right. A cultivated person establishes the inner life through respect and care, then gives external behavior a reliable form through justice. When reverence and righteousness work together, good character is not isolated from action or from other people. The description of being straight, square, and great therefore concerns more than a set of abstract virtues. It portrays someone whose convictions, decisions, and outward behavior fit together so consistently that action need not be accompanied by uncertainty.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-04
translation.text: Even when receptive strength possesses fine qualities, it may keep them inward rather than display them. In service to the ruler, it helps a larger undertaking reach completion without claiming all the credit. The original passage presents this through the traditional roles of earth, wife, and minister, each understood as assisting a larger process. These are descriptions of a historical model of complementary functions, not a requirement that modern people accept its social hierarchy. Within that framework, Kun's virtue is to support successful completion without insisting on personal prominence.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-05
translation.text: When heaven and earth interact, plants and trees flourish; when that interaction closes, worthy people may withdraw from public life. The saying about closing a bag's opening describes caution at a time when open action would be unwise. It promises neither applause nor a spectacular achievement: it speaks of avoiding blame even if no reputation is gained. The commentary links restraint to the conditions of the age. A thoughtful person may need to protect integrity by speaking less and declining involvement until circumstances become more favorable.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-06
translation.text: Yellow symbolizes balance at the center. The cultivated person is inwardly centered, understands principles clearly, and occupies a fitting position. Goodness is not confined to thought: it becomes visible in bodily conduct and then in public work. The passage moves from inner qualities to outward expression, showing how coherent character affects what a person does. This is called the highest form of beauty because personal values and practical deeds are not separated. The imagery belongs to the traditional symbolism of Kun, where inward steadiness supports effective action.

translation.title: Words on the Lines / WENYAN WENYAN-02-07
translation.text: When yin becomes so powerful that it rivals yang, conflict emerges. The commentary explains why the related line speaks of dragons and blood: the dragon acknowledges the opposing yang force, while blood indicates that yin has not ceased to belong to its own kind. The mingling colors, dark and yellow, symbolize heaven and earth interwoven in the struggle. The passage is a traditional account of complementary forces becoming antagonistic when balance is lost. It describes the imagery of a dangerous extreme rather than celebrating the conflict itself.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-01-01
translation.text: The passage begins with heaven above and earth below as a way of describing the distinct but related roles of Qian and Kun. Movement and stillness, strength and yielding, and the grouping of things by kind make differences and change visible. Thunder, rain, wind, sunlight, and the alternating seasons give concrete examples. Qian is associated with initiating life, while Kun brings things into form. The author then emphasizes ease and simplicity: what is clear can be understood and trusted, and what is straightforward can be practiced effectively. Understanding these principles allows people to find their place within the larger order of heaven and earth.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-02-01
translation.text: The sages established hexagrams by observing images and added statements to distinguish favorable and unfavorable situations. As firm and yielding lines interact, circumstances change. Good fortune and misfortune describe gain and loss; regret and difficulty warn of emerging problems; advance and retreat are different expressions of change. The six lines connect patterns associated with heaven, earth, and human life. A thoughtful person studies the arrangement of the Changes in quiet times and attends to the words attached to each line. When action is required, the person also considers changing lines and divination, seeking a responsible response rather than treating one judgment as unchangeable.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-03-01
translation.text: This passage explains the different functions of the text. The judgment on a hexagram describes its overall image, while individual lines show movement and changing conditions. Good or bad fortune concerns possible gains and losses; regret and difficulty point to smaller faults or warning signs. “No blame” does not mean that mistakes never happen: it means that errors can be recognized and repaired appropriately. Positions distinguish higher and lower roles, while the hexagram as a whole shows the scale of the situation. Its words may sound reassuring or dangerous because they point toward different possible outcomes. Interpretation must therefore consider position, context, and the direction of change together.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-04-01
translation.text: The Changes is presented as a way of understanding patterns in heaven, earth, and human existence. Looking upward to celestial phenomena and downward to the terrain reveals both visible and hidden processes. Reflecting on beginnings and endings encourages thought about life and death; references to vital energy, wandering spirits, and divine beings reflect the ancient intellectual world of the text. Its ideal is not to withdraw from people but to understand many things without excess, act with compassion, and remain at ease with one's circumstances. Change has no single permanent shape: like day becoming night, its operations must be recognized through the particular situation rather than reduced to one fixed formula.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-05-01
translation.text: The familiar expression “one yin and one yang is called the Way” describes reality as an ongoing relationship between complementary forces. What carries this movement forward is called goodness, and what becomes established within living beings is called their nature. Different observers may recognize compassion or wisdom in the same process, while everyday users may not notice it at all. The passage links great achievement with abundance and great virtue with continual renewal. “Change” means life generating more life. Qian forms initiating images; Kun follows and completes them. Divination explores what may come, practical affairs require adaptability, and the mysterious character of yin and yang is described as spirit.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-06-01
translation.text: The Changes is called vast because its patterns apply both to remote and nearby things. Considered on a grand scale, it reaches beyond any obvious boundary; considered closely, it can be quiet, precise, and orderly. Qian is described as concentrated when still and direct when active, the source of great beginnings. Kun gathers when still and opens when active, giving wide scope for things to develop. These two qualities complement each other rather than compete. The text compares their breadth to heaven and earth, their adaptability to the seasons, and yin and yang to the sun and moon. Ease and simplicity are treated as expressions of exceptional virtue.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-07-01
translation.text: Confucius is quoted as praising the Changes as a profound resource for cultivating character and enlarging worthy undertakings. Wisdom should aspire upward, like heaven, while proper conduct should remain humble, like earth. The point is not to choose intellect over courtesy or humility over achievement. A mature person needs both: expansive understanding and grounded behavior. Heaven and earth each have their position, and the movement of change unfolds between them. By repeatedly preserving and refining one's own moral nature, a person enters the path of duty and right conduct. The passage thus approaches the Changes as a guide to ethical development, not merely a collection of predictions.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-01
translation.text: The sages perceived complexities in the world and fashioned images resembling the appropriate features of things. Such images became the symbolic language of the Changes. They also observed movement, relationships, and recurring patterns; the lines and their statements describe these developments and distinguish favorable from unfavorable directions. The text claims that even difficult realities can be represented without becoming impossible to understand, and constant movement can be discussed without losing order. Its closing advice is practical: compare and examine a situation before speaking, and deliberate before acting. Careful interpretation and discussion help people respond to change instead of reacting to appearances alone.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-02
translation.text: A crane calling from a hidden place is answered by its young, suggesting that genuine words can be heard far beyond their source. The passage explains that good speech may inspire people even a thousand miles away, while harmful speech can drive them away. Words and actions are a pivot on which honor and disgrace turn, so they demand care. The second quotation, from Fellowship with Others, moves from crying to laughter. People may serve or withdraw, speak or remain silent, yet two people who truly share one purpose can overcome formidable obstacles. Their agreement is likened to a fragrance as pleasing as orchids.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-03
translation.text: The line about placing an offering on white thatch illustrates exceptional care. An offering could simply be set on the ground, yet placing a thin layer of clean grass beneath it shows additional respect. The grass itself is ordinary and inexpensive, but its use in the right setting carries weight. The lesson is not that elaborate ceremony is always necessary. Rather, attention to a small detail can reveal the seriousness with which an important duty is undertaken. If this attitude of thoughtful preparation is extended to other activities, unnecessary errors become less likely. The text connects prudence in a simple ritual act with steadiness in broader conduct.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-04
translation.text: The passage interprets the line about a hardworking yet modest person who reaches a good conclusion. Such a person has accomplishments but does not advertise them, and contributes without claiming every result as personal merit. The text calls this depth of character. Virtue concerns the fullness of one's inner qualities, while ritual propriety concerns the respectful manner in which those qualities are expressed. Modesty does not erase achievement; it prevents success from turning into arrogance. Someone who can lower themselves in relation to others despite real accomplishments is better able to preserve trust and standing. The line therefore links sustained success with humility rather than display.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-05
translation.text: The expression “a dragon that rises too high has cause for regret” is explained through the isolation of an exalted person. Someone may appear powerful yet lack a secure role, stand above others without public support, and fail to receive help from capable people below. Height alone is not effective leadership. When a person is cut off from colleagues, advisers, and those affected by decisions, even a seemingly strong position becomes unstable. Acting forcefully under such conditions is likely to bring regret. The image of the overreaching dragon warns about the danger of success carried beyond its proper limits, not about ambition in every circumstance.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-06
translation.text: The advice not to step beyond the inner courtyard is connected here with discretion in speech. Disorder often begins when words disclose matters that should have remained confidential. If a ruler cannot keep confidence, ministers may be lost; if a minister is indiscreet, personal safety may be endangered; if sensitive plans leak too early, a valuable undertaking may fail. The passage does not praise silence in every situation. It distinguishes the right time to speak from situations requiring careful restraint. A cultivated person weighs responsibility, audience, and timing before sharing information. Guarding words becomes part of preserving trust and enabling important work to reach completion.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-08-07
translation.text: This passage uses the image of someone carrying a burden while riding a distinguished carriage to discuss social roles and the attraction of thieves. In its ancient hierarchy, a carriage could signal status that the rider had not earned, inviting others to seize it. Arrogance above and aggression below can likewise provoke conflict.
