The text adds that careless storage attracts theft and ostentatious display invites improper attention. These claims reflect historical moral assumptions and should not be taken as excuses for wrongdoing. The central interpretive point is that visible behavior, mismatched responsibilities, and neglected precautions can create avoidable risks. The Changes asks readers to examine the conditions surrounding trouble.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-09-01
translation.text: The passage lays out an ancient numerical account of divination. Odd numbers one, three, five, seven, and nine belong to heaven and total twenty-five; even numbers two, four, six, eight, and ten belong to earth and total thirty. Together they make fifty-five. In the great expansion method, fifty yarrow stalks are counted but forty-nine are used. They are divided into two groups to symbolize the two primary powers; one stalk is set aside to represent a third element. Counting in fours evokes the four seasons, and the remainders evoke intercalary months. These are symbolic procedures within the classical divination system, not a description of modern probability theory.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-09-02
translation.text: Here the text calculates the number of yarrow-stalk values associated with Qian and Kun. Qian's six lines amount to 216, and Kun's to 144, making 360, a number compared with the days of a traditional year. Across the two parts of the Changes, the total is given as 11,520, symbolically associated with the multitude of things. Four operations complete a change, and eighteen changes produce a hexagram. From the eight foundational trigrams, the method can be extended to many combinations and situations. The author treats numerical procedures as a disciplined way to disclose patterns of transformation, while the invocation of spirits belongs to its ancient worldview.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-01
translation.text: The text identifies four ways the sages use the Changes. For speech and interpretation, they value its written statements; for action, they attend to transformation; for designing objects, they study images; and for divination, they consider the resulting judgments. A cultivated person who faces a decision can consult the system as though asking a question and receiving an answering echo. Its traditional description emphasizes that distance or obscurity need not prevent a meaningful response. This is a claim within the classical theory of divination, not proof that every future event can be predicted. The broader lesson is that words, images, changing circumstances, and practical choices serve distinct but connected roles.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-02
translation.text: The passage describes combining and recombining numbers to perceive transformation. By comparing patterns and arranging them in different relationships, the diviner seeks the structures that make phenomena intelligible. Extending numerical operations to their limits is said to establish the images through which the world can be represented. The text admires the ability of the Changes to hold variation and structure together: the combinations are not arbitrary figures but part of an ordered symbolic system. It calls this extraordinary adaptability. In reading the passage, it is useful to distinguish its historical philosophical claim about numerical symbolism from a modern scientific claim about the causes of events.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-03
translation.text: The Changes is described as having neither private thoughts nor deliberate actions. It remains still and silent, yet when approached through its method, it is said to respond and disclose the underlying reasons for things. The emphasis is on the contrast between inactivity and meaningful response. Unlike a human adviser, the classic is not imagined as pursuing interests or making choices of its own. In the traditional account, its symbolic arrangement becomes informative through the encounter between a question and a changing pattern. The author calls this mysterious, even divine. Readers can understand the passage as expressing the perceived depth of divination without treating the claim as an established physical mechanism.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-04
translation.text: The Changes is portrayed as a means by which sages investigate both the deepest principles and the first, almost invisible signs of events. Because their inquiry reaches deeply, they can understand people's intentions; because they notice early indications, they can address difficult affairs before they grow. Its work is described as so subtle that it seems to act quickly without haste and arrive without travel. These striking phrases celebrate insight into connected processes, not literal movement across space. The passage joins patient study with timely action. It suggests that a decision becomes more effective when one understands broad conditions and recognizes small changes before they become obvious.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-10-05
translation.text: This short sentence looks back to the earlier statement that the Changes contains four ways of the sages. Those four are the use of words to express meaning, the use of transformations to guide action, the use of images in forming objects, and the use of divinatory judgments in consultation. The author is closing an argument rather than introducing a new list. The surrounding discussion explains why each function matters: language clarifies, change reveals timing, images connect ideas with forms, and divination gives a traditional framework for considering uncertainty. The sentence should therefore be read as a conclusion to the preceding passage, not as an independent prediction.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-11-01
translation.text: This long passage asks what the Changes is for and answers that it opens understanding, helps accomplish affairs, and embraces the patterns of the world. It describes yarrow stalks, hexagrams, and six lines as complementary ways of examining uncertainty. The sages are said to purify their minds and share the people's concern for fortune and misfortune. Closing a door symbolizes Kun; opening it symbolizes Qian; their alternation is change, and ceaseless movement is continuity. From the Supreme Ultimate arise two modes, then four images and eight trigrams. Instruments, laws, and human undertakings emerge as patterns are given practical form. References to spirits, the River Chart, and the Luo Writing belong to the classical tradition.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-12-01
translation.text: “Helped by heaven, auspicious, with nothing unfavorable” is explained through the meaning of help itself. According to the passage, heaven assists those who act in accord with its patterns, while people assist those who can be trusted. A person should therefore cultivate sincerity, think carefully about the direction of events, and honor capable and virtuous people. Assistance is not presented simply as an arbitrary gift. It arises from fitting one's conduct to a wider order and establishing reliable relationships. The language of heaven's support reflects the text's moral cosmology; its practical emphasis is on trustworthiness, responsiveness, and respect for good judgment.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-12-02
translation.text: Confucius is quoted as saying that writing cannot express every spoken thought and speech cannot exhaust everything in the mind. Does that mean the sages' intentions are inaccessible? The passage answers no. The sages established images to carry meanings beyond literal language, arranged hexagrams to show the complexity of human feelings and appearances, and attached statements to make their teaching clearer. They then explored how change could be understood and applied. Images, words, and transformations work together rather than replacing one another. The passage is an important account of why the Changes uses symbolic figures alongside written explanations: some insights need more than a verbal definition.

translation.title: Appended Statements I / XICI-U XICI-U-12-03
translation.text: Qian and Kun are presented as the fundamental conditions that allow the Changes to appear. The text distinguishes the Way, which lies beyond particular physical forms, from concrete vessels and instruments, which take recognizable shape. Adapting and reshaping circumstances is called change; extending an effective pattern into action is called continuity or practical connection. When such understanding benefits people, it becomes an undertaking. The sages form images from complex realities and write line statements about events and their outcomes. Yet the final source of effective interpretation is not the diagram alone. The passage says that profound understanding depends on the person, and trustworthy achievement rests on cultivated character.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-01-01
translation.text: The eight trigrams present images; stacking them creates six lines through which changing situations may be considered. Firm and yielding lines interact, and judgments of good fortune, misfortune, regret, and difficulty arise through action. Qian exemplifies a clear initiative, while Kun exemplifies receptive simplicity. The passage then connects governance to life: nurturing living things is Heaven and Earth's great virtue, while a ruler preserves legitimate authority through humanity, resources, truthful speech, and justice.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-01
translation.text: The text attributes the invention of the eight trigrams to Fuxi, who observed the sky, land, animals, the human body, and surrounding objects. The trigrams classify patterns seen in nature and human life. It also describes how people made knotted nets for fishing and hunting, associating this practical invention with the Li trigram. The account is a traditional explanation of cultural origins, not a modern archaeological chronology.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-02
translation.text: After Fuxi, the culture hero Shennong is said to have fashioned wooden ploughing tools and taught agriculture. He also gathered people and goods at a midday market so that exchange could meet practical needs. The narrative associates improved farming with the Yi hexagram and organized exchange with Shi He. It presents inventions as ways of relieving human difficulty and gives hexagram images an explanatory role in cultural memory.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-03
translation.text: The account next credits the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun with accommodating social change rather than exhausting people through rigid rule. When a method reaches its limit, it must change; change opens a path, and a workable path can endure. Their orderly government, figured by their hanging garments, is associated with Qian and Kun. This is the familiar principle that adaptation makes continuity possible.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-04
translation.text: People hollowed logs into boats and shaped wood into oars. These implements allowed travelers and goods to cross waters that previously separated communities, extending benefits to distant places. The text links the invention to Huan, a hexagram concerned with dispersing obstructions and restoring communication. The point is practical: a well-designed tool can remove a barrier and connect what had been isolated.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-05
translation.text: Tamed cattle and horses could carry heavy loads across long distances, extending the range of human work and travel. The text associates this development with Sui, following or adapting. It also describes fortified gates and night watches with wooden clappers to prepare for intruders, linking these precautions to Yu. Mobility and security appear side by side as complementary requirements of settled communities.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-06
translation.text: The invention of mortar and pestle is described in very concrete terms: wood is cut into a pounding implement, and a hollow is made to receive grain. Grinding and pounding make staple food easier to prepare for many households. The passage associates this useful technique with Xiao Guo. The traditional analogy connects small, carefully directed actions with tangible benefits in everyday life.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-07
translation.text: A wooden bow was bent into shape and arrows were sharpened for its use. These tools provided an ability to defend or exert power over a distance, changing the balance of force between people. The passage associates their invention with Kui, a hexagram of divergence. It records an ancient account of technology and authority rather than endorsing armed coercion as a present-day moral rule.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-08
translation.text: The earliest people are pictured as living in caves or in the open. Later generations built houses with beams and roofs that offered shelter from wind and rain. The narrative links the development of durable buildings with Da Zhuang, great strength. It shows how the classical text uses hexagram qualities to illuminate a transition from exposure to organized habitation.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-09
translation.text: The passage contrasts an early burial practice, in which bodies were wrapped in brushwood and placed in the countryside, with later funerary customs using inner and outer coffins. It notes that early graves lacked formal mounds, planted markers, or fixed mourning periods. The transition to more elaborate burial is associated with Da Guo. This is a traditional historical narrative of the growing formality of ritual.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-02-10
translation.text: Knotted cords once helped communities keep records and administer affairs. Later rulers are said to have introduced written signs and contracts, enabling officials to manage duties and ordinary people to verify arrangements. This innovation is associated with Guai, the hexagram of decisive clarification. The underlying thought is that reliable documentation makes public decisions and obligations more understandable.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-03-01
translation.text: The text explains why the Changes speaks through images. An image resembles something observed; the Tuan commentary considers the overall capacities of a hexagram, while individual lines imitate movement and changing circumstances. Fortune and misfortune, regret and difficulty, become recognizable within this framework. Rather than treating symbols as literal photographs of events, readers are asked to consider what kind of situation an image represents.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-03-02
translation.text: The passage discusses why certain trigrams are classed as yang despite containing two yin lines, while others are classed as yin despite containing two yang lines. It uses odd and even patterns as its organizing principle. One ruler with two subjects is described as a stable arrangement, while two rulers with one subject illustrates divided authority. These judgments reflect the text's traditional political hierarchy, not a modern claim about people's worth.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-01
translation.text: The passage begins by questioning restless speculation. Different roads can reach a shared destination, just as the sun and moon alternate and the seasons succeed one another. Withdrawal and extension work together: a caterpillar contracts before advancing, and snakes and dragons withdraw to preserve life. Understanding the underlying principle is useful only when put into practice. The ideal is to respond skillfully to recurring patterns rather than remain caught in endless worry.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-02
translation.text: Quoting a line about being trapped among rocks and thorns, Confucius warns against clinging to an inappropriate position or relying on what cannot support us. Such choices expose a person to disgrace and danger. The image of returning home unable to find one's wife emphasizes the severity of the consequences. The commentary asks readers to examine whether a chosen place or support is genuinely suitable.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-03
translation.text: The image of a nobleman shooting a hawk from a high wall becomes a lesson about preparation and timing. The hawk is the target, the bow and arrow are instruments, and the archer must have the skill to use them. A cultivated person keeps abilities ready and acts only when the opportunity is right. Effective action follows from preparation; hurried movement without the proper means is not the ideal.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-04
translation.text: This passage considers how small habits accumulate. It portrays people who ignore minor wrongdoing unless a penalty forces them to stop, and who dismiss small good actions as insignificant. Yet repeated misconduct eventually becomes difficult to conceal or correct. The images of restraints on toes and ears mark early and late consequences. The moral argument is that correction should begin while an error is still manageable.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-05
translation.text: Prosperity can create the illusion that danger has disappeared. Confucius therefore urges the cultivated person to remember peril while secure, possible loss while thriving, and disorder while governing peacefully. The image of something tied securely to mulberry roots emphasizes vigilance and sound foundations. Stability is maintained not by assuming it will last automatically, but by attending to what might undermine it.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-06
translation.text: A person of weak character holding high office, limited knowledge planning vast affairs, or insufficient strength carrying a heavy burden is exposed to failure. The image of a ritual cauldron breaking its legs and spilling food dramatizes responsibility exceeding capacity. The lesson is to match duties to competence and resources. Prestigious position alone cannot make an unsuitable appointment successful.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-07
translation.text: To perceive the smallest beginnings of change is presented as a rare form of discernment. A cultivated person neither flatters superiors nor belittles subordinates, noticing early signs before they become obvious. The image of a firmness like stone means that once the situation is understood, one need not delay an entire day. Sound judgment combines attention to the subtle with timely, decisive action.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-08
translation.text: Confucius praises Yan Hui for detecting his own mistakes quickly and refusing to repeat them. This is the idea of returning before one has wandered far from the proper path. The passage then compares concentration to the generative meeting of Heaven and Earth and speaks of companions joining or separating. Its common concern is unity of purpose: scattered intentions are less effective than a clear commitment.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-04-09
translation.text: Before acting, a cultivated person establishes secure footing; before speaking, a calm mind; before asking others for help, a stable relationship. People do not readily support reckless action, frightened speech, or demands unsupported by trust. The quoted line about receiving no benefit and instead being attacked warns of these failures. The commentary presents patience and sound human relations as prerequisites for effective action.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-05-01
translation.text: Qian and Kun are described as the gateway to understanding change. Their contrasting qualities of yang and yin, strength and yielding, give structure to natural and human events. The text says that the Changes recalls the past, clarifies hidden patterns, and helps distinguish appearances from realities. Its images may be small, but the classes of situations they suggest are broad. Meaning comes from applying an image carefully, not from the name alone.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-01
translation.text: The author asks whether the Changes arose in an era of serious anxiety. This brief introductory statement sets the context for a discussion of virtues learned under pressure. Rather than presenting the classic as the product of effortless prosperity, it invites the reader to see the following lessons as responses to uncertainty and danger. Its historical attribution is posed as a question within the tradition.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-02
translation.text: Nine hexagrams are presented as foundations for moral cultivation. Lu concerns the basis of conduct, Qian humility, Fu a return to one's roots, Heng steadiness, Sun correction, Yi enrichment, Kun discernment in hardship, Jing a stable place of support, and Xun measured adjustment. The passage makes a compact index of ethical themes; each quality has its role in developing judgment over time.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-03
translation.text: The same nine hexagrams are described through their practical effects. Proper conduct reaches harmony; humility makes dignity brighter; returning allows small distinctions to be recognized; constancy persists amid complexity. Reduction begins with difficulty but can lead to ease, while increase nurtures growth. Confinement can teach a path through hardship, the well serves others while staying in place, and gentleness works with measured restraint.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-06-04
translation.text: Here the nine hexagrams are turned into methods of action. Lu guides harmonious behavior, Qian establishes courtesy, Fu encourages self-knowledge, and Heng maintains a consistent virtue. Sun helps remove harm; Yi promotes benefits; Kun limits resentment; Jing clarifies what is right; and Xun teaches flexible judgment. The repeated catalog is intentional: the same symbols are examined as virtues, effects, and practical uses.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-07-01
translation.text: The Changes should remain close to lived experience because situations do not remain fixed. Firm and yielding lines shift through the six positions, so a reader cannot apply one rigid rule to every moment. The text calls for proportionate movement and withdrawal, awareness of danger, and respectful attention to the words of the hexagrams. Yet insight requires the right person to act upon it; principles alone do not carry themselves into practice.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-07-02
translation.text: To understand a hexagram, follow a situation from its beginning to its conclusion. The first line is often difficult to interpret because causes are just emerging; the top line is easier to assess because consequences are clearer. The middle lines fill in the course of development and reveal differences of conduct and position. The text suggests first examining the overall Tuan judgment before interpreting the individual stages.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-08-01
translation.text: The second and fourth lines may have similar roles but different risks: the second often receives praise, while the fourth is uneasy because it lies close to the ruler's position. The third and fifth likewise differ, with the fifth more likely to accomplish something and the third exposed to danger. These observations use the traditional hierarchy of line positions. No line can be evaluated solely by whether it is firm or yielding.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-08-02
translation.text: A six-line hexagram is explained as a representation of Heaven, Earth, and humanity, each considered in two aspects. The resulting six places depict changing relationships rather than six identical units. Lines differ in level, and their interactions create patterned meaning. When their qualities and positions do not suit one another, unfavorable outcomes may appear. The scheme integrates the three domains into one interpretive framework.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-08-03
translation.text: The text situates the rise of the Changes in the troubled transition from late Shang to early Zhou and the conflict involving King Wen and the Shang ruler Zhou. That setting explains why many judgments sound cautious or dangerous. Awareness of peril can lead toward safety; careless assumptions of ease may bring collapse. The central recommendation is vigilance throughout the course of an undertaking, with avoiding serious blame as the goal.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-09-01
translation.text: Qian represents unsurpassed strength, yet its clear virtue allows dangers to be recognized; Kun represents deep responsiveness, and its simplicity helps one notice obstacles. Images, signs, and divination are used to discuss changing conditions and possible outcomes. The text does not separate insight from conduct: awareness of movement is meant to encourage careful action, not merely fascination with signs.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-09-02
translation.text: Heaven and Earth provide the setting in which human planning and divination are brought together. Trigrams communicate through images, and Tuan and line texts describe situations and emotions. As firmness and yielding interact, judgments of advantage, danger, regret, and loss can change. Love and dislike, distance and closeness, sincerity and deception all shape relations. Even people standing near each other may suffer when they cannot work together.

translation.title: Appended Statements II / XICI-L XICI-L-09-03
translation.text: Different states of mind appear through speech. Someone preparing betrayal may speak with embarrassment, while inner uncertainty produces tangled explanations. A settled and principled person tends to be concise; an impatient person speaks excessively. Malicious accusations wander, and a person who has lost integrity becomes evasive. These are traditional observations about rhetoric and character, not infallible tests for judging individuals.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-01-01
translation.text: The sages are said to have used yarrow-stalk divination to investigate hidden patterns. Numerical relationships of Heaven and Earth, changes between yin and yang, and the interplay of firm and yielding lines gave rise to trigrams and individual lines. The text describes this system as a way of connecting reflection on nature with moral conduct and a sense of life's larger order.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-02-01
translation.text: The three powers are Heaven, Earth, and humanity. Heaven is discussed through yin and yang, Earth through yielding and firmness, and human affairs through humaneness and rightness. By treating each power in two aspects, the text accounts for the six lines of a hexagram. This is an interpretive design, not a claim that human relationships have only six possible forms.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-03-01
translation.text: Heaven and Earth take their positions; mountains and lakes exchange influences; thunder and wind interact; water and fire stand in complementary tension. The eight trigrams are arranged together to consider patterns already known and changes yet to emerge. The text contrasts reviewing the past with reasoning toward the future, explaining the distinctive direction of interpretation in the Changes.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-04-01
translation.text: Thunder stirs things to movement, wind disperses, rain nourishes, and sunlight warms. Gen brings a halt, Dui brings joy, Qian provides direction, and Kun receives and stores. The passage identifies differing functions within one evolving natural process. No single force performs every task; generation, distribution, growth, completion, and rest each require their proper role.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-01
translation.text: The passage follows an ordered cycle through the eight trigrams. Life begins to stir in Zhen, becomes orderly in Xun, appears in the brightness of Li, and is nurtured through Kun. Dui marks joy in maturity, Qian contesting forces, Kan labor and return, and Gen completion that permits another beginning. This is a symbolic arrangement of time and direction.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-02
translation.text: Zhen is assigned to the east, the direction where things begin to emerge. The statement belongs to a larger directional sequence connecting the eight trigrams with changes in the natural year. Its emphasis is the first stirring of life rather than a rule about the geographical east in every context.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-03
translation.text: Xun is assigned to the southeast, where developing things become orderly and distinct. The word for becoming aligned suggests growth attaining a coordinated form. Within the directional sequence, this is a stage after initial emergence in Zhen and before the full visibility associated with Li.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-04
translation.text: Li signifies brightness and is placed in the south. In daylight, things become visible to one another. The traditional image of a ruler facing south to govern draws on this connection with clarity and illumination. The passage uses direction and light to express a model of public awareness and effective rule.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-05
translation.text: Kun represents the Earth as the receptive ground on which living things are nourished. The phrase describes the work of life being sustained by the capacity of the ground to carry and support it. The point is not inactivity but the ongoing labor of giving things the conditions in which they can mature.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-06
translation.text: Dui corresponds to the height of autumn, when crops and other products of the year reach maturity. It is associated with pleasure or satisfaction. In the seasonal pattern, joy follows the effort of growth and gathering; the text treats that delight as one recognizable feature of the Dui trigram.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-07
translation.text: Qian is placed in the northwest in this directional arrangement. The phrase about battle refers to yin and yang drawing against each other as the seasons turn. It depicts an energetic change of balance rather than a literal prediction of war in that geographic direction.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-08
translation.text: Kan signifies water and is placed in the north. It is connected with labor, difficulty, and the return of living things to a hidden or resting condition. Within the yearly cycle, northern darkness and winter activity suggest preservation through a demanding phase.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-05-09
translation.text: Gen occupies the northeast. It is the position where things finish one phase and become ready to begin another. Stopping is therefore not the opposite of all growth: a genuine ending may also be the condition for renewal. The passage makes Gen the hinge between completion and fresh emergence.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-01
translation.text: The word shen, often translated as spirit or the marvelous, is used here to describe the extraordinary subtlety of transformation. The passage is concerned with effects that are apparent even when their workings cannot easily be traced. It should be understood within the text's philosophical and cosmological vocabulary.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-02
translation.text: No force brings such sudden movement among things as thunder. Its sound and impact make it a vivid emblem of the start of change. In the sequence of natural forces, thunder represents activation rather than the full development or completion that follows.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-03
translation.text: Wind is presented as the force that most readily bends, stirs, and disperses things. Its movement is less abrupt than thunder but reaches widely. The classical comparison uses wind to show how influence can enter many places without needing a single direct blow.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-04
translation.text: Fire is described as the strongest of these familiar forces for drying things. The passage identifies a particular observable action of heat, not the entire meaning of Li. Such simple natural observations provide the vocabulary for the larger system of corresponding images.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-05
translation.text: The lake or marsh is connected with delight and refreshment. Dui's association with joy grows out of the way water-filled lowlands can sustain and enliven living things. The passage names one recognizable quality of that image as part of the trigram's broader symbolic range.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-06
translation.text: Water is named the great moistening and nourishing force. Its ability to soak the earth and support growth supplies the comparison. The text gives water this particular function within the complementary forces of nature, while other passages also use it as an image of danger and depth.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-07
translation.text: Gen has a distinctive role at the boundary between ending and beginning. Mountains and stopping express completion, but completion also allows another course to start. In the broader passage, Gen closes a cycle without implying that transformation itself has ceased forever.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-06-08
translation.text: Water and fire interact, thunder and wind do not cancel each other, and mountains and lakes exchange influence. Together these contrasting forces make transformation possible and bring things to completion. The passage stresses coexistence and coordination rather than reducing nature to a single element.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-07-01
translation.text: This sentence offers a concise glossary for the eight trigrams: Qian is vigor, Kun receptivity, Zhen movement, Xun penetration, Kan danger or a pit, Li attachment, Gen stopping, and Dui delight. These are central associations for interpreting images; they are not complete definitions for every use of each trigram.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-08-01
translation.text: The trigrams are matched with animals: Qian with the horse, Kun the ox, Zhen the dragon, Xun the rooster, Kan the pig, Li the pheasant, Gen the dog, and Dui the sheep. Such correspondences illustrate how the same eight symbols were used to organize several different fields of observation.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-09-01
translation.text: A second series connects each trigram with a body part. Qian represents the head; Kun, the abdomen; Zhen, the feet; Xun, the thighs; Kan, the ears; Li, the eyes; Gen, the hands; and Dui, the mouth. These are conventional symbolic associations in the text, not anatomical or medical diagnoses.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-10-01
translation.text: The eight trigrams are arranged as a family: Qian and Kun stand for father and mother. Zhen and Xun represent eldest son and daughter, Kan and Li the middle son and daughter, and Gen and Dui the youngest son and daughter. The names express how yin and yang lines are situated within the three-line figures.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-01
translation.text: Qian is associated with heaven, circularity, the ruler and father, jade and metal, cold and ice, deep red, several kinds of horse, and fruit growing on trees. This catalog records an expansive system of images. Its purpose is to show how firmness and height can be recognized through diverse objects.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-02
translation.text: Kun's associations include earth, mother, cloth, a cooking vessel, thrift, even distribution, a cow with its calf, a large vehicle, patterned form, a multitude, and a handle. These images emphasize carrying, receiving, providing, and sustaining. The list should be kept as a traditional symbolic inventory.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-03
translation.text: In the continuation of Kun's associations, the color black is assigned to it when considering the Earth. This brief statement completes a longer catalog. It is a conventional image within the trigram tradition rather than a literal statement about the color of all soil.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-04
translation.text: Zhen is connected with thunder and dragon, dark-yellow color, unfolding, broad roads, eldest sons, quick movement, young green bamboo, and reeds. The list gathers things marked by stirring, emergence, and energetic growth. The diversity of items shows that associations are analogies, not single literal definitions.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-05
translation.text: In describing horses, the Zhen image is associated with loud neighing, a distinctive hoof or leg, and a marked forehead. These concrete animal features extend Zhen's wider association with visible activity and strong movement. Some traditional animal terms are textually difficult, so their details require specialized philological review.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-06
translation.text: For growing crops, Zhen is associated with shoots that emerge in an inverted or unusual fashion. The description is part of a catalog of natural images connected with this trigram. It illustrates the ancient habit of identifying distinctive forms of growth as symbolic parallels.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-07
translation.text: The concluding characteristics ascribed to Zhen are vigor and lush freshness. After its many images of thunder, animals, and plants, the catalog returns to the qualities of forceful beginning and flourishing growth. These words should be read as imagery rather than as a prediction about a specific event.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-08
translation.text: Xun is associated with wood, wind, the eldest daughter, a straight measuring line, craftsmen, white, length, height, advancing and retreating, indecision, and scent. Its recurring idea is influence that enters or extends through things. The catalog includes both physical attributes and patterns of conduct.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-09
translation.text: In human appearance, Xun is associated with sparse hair, a broad forehead, and conspicuous whites of the eyes. The text also mentions a threefold gain in the marketplace. This is an old catalog of images extending from bodily signs to commerce, and it is not a validated way to predict an individual's characteristics or income.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-10
translation.text: The final association in this Xun sequence is an agitated or restless quality. Although Xun is often described as gentle penetration, the catalog also allows for instability and repeated movement. Its symbolism is broader than a simple equation of gentleness with passivity.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-11
translation.text: Kan is associated with water, ditches and channels, concealment, bending and straightening, bows, and wheels. These images have to do with depth, flow, difficulty, and shaped movement. Their diversity reflects the use of the trigram as a network of analogies rather than a literal inventory of water-related objects.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-12
translation.text: When applied to people, Kan is associated with added anxiety, heart trouble, ear pain, blood, and red coloring. These are part of a historical divinatory symbolism and should not be interpreted as medically reliable symptom predictions. The commentary records the associations without treating them as clinical facts.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-13
translation.text: For horses, Kan is linked to a fine back, anxious disposition, a lowered head, thin hooves, and dragging movement. The list extends the trigram's themes of tension and difficulty to recognizable animal features. Its terms preserve an older descriptive vocabulary that may have variant scholarly interpretations.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-14
translation.text: When applied to a vehicle, Kan is associated with many defects; the same textual sequence also names passage, the moon, and theft. The varying kinds of images show a broad associative method. They should be presented as listed by the classical source, rather than forced into a single modern explanation.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-15
translation.text: For trees, Kan is associated with wood that is hard and dense at its center. This brief image adds another material property to the trigram's catalog. The link lies in the idea of a strong inner core enclosed within a more vulnerable exterior.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-16
translation.text: Li is associated with fire, the sun, lightning, the middle daughter, armor, and weapons. Brightness, visibility, and protective or dangerous instruments appear together in this symbolic list. It captures the varied uses of the fire image in ritual, observation, and human affairs.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-17
translation.text: The source continues with a difficult list attached to Li, including a large belly and several shelled creatures such as turtles, crabs, and shellfish. Its wording also contains a potentially problematic item in the supplied base text. The images have been retained at a general descriptive level pending specialist textual collation.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-18
translation.text: For trees, Li is linked with an upper portion that has become dry or withered. The image connects brightness and heat with a visible condition of wood. This is a particular entry in the traditional symbolism, not a universal botanical classification.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-19
translation.text: Gen is associated with mountains, pathways, small stones, gates, fruit, gatekeepers, fingers, dogs, mice, and creatures with dark beaks. Many examples suggest boundaries, thresholds, firmness, or stopping places. The passage uses natural and social objects to expand the trigram's range.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-20
translation.text: For wood, Gen describes hardness and many joints or knots. The image fits its wider association with mountains, firmness, and distinct points where movement is checked. It is one item in a symbolic correspondence system, not a technical definition of timber.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-21
translation.text: Dui is linked to marshes, the youngest daughter, shamans, mouth and speech, breaking, and separation. Its range joins pleasurable expression with openings and divisions. The association with speech helps explain why other passages connect Dui with joyful communication and persuasion.

translation.title: Explaining the Trigrams / SHUOGUA SHUOGUA-11-22
translation.text: In the final entries, Dui is associated with hard salty soil, a secondary wife, and sheep. The passage continues an old image system in which natural environments, domestic roles, and animals can all exemplify a trigram. These historic categories are best preserved with their original context.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-01
translation.text: Heaven and Earth provide the setting in which the myriad things come into being. The sequence begins with this broad account of generation before describing particular stages of growth.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-02
translation.text: Once living things fill the space between Heaven and Earth, the sequence moves to Zhun. Its difficulty and fullness describe the crowded, uncertain first moments of emerging life.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-03
translation.text: Things newly born are still immature and uncomprehending, so Meng follows Zhun. The transition turns from initial emergence to the need for instruction and enlightenment.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-04
translation.text: Young life needs nourishment. Xu therefore follows Meng and is explained through eating and drinking, which sustain growth before more complicated social activities arise.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-05
translation.text: The need to obtain and distribute food can create competing claims. Song, contention or litigation, follows Xu as the sequence moves from nourishment to dispute.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-06
translation.text: Disputes can summon groups of people into collective action. Shi follows Song because its name refers to an assembled multitude, including an army.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-07
translation.text: A gathering needs relationships of support and alignment. Bi follows Shi to represent people drawing close to one another after forming a larger group.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-08
translation.text: Once people are allied, they can begin to accumulate limited resources. Xiao Xu follows Bi and describes a modest process of restraint and gathering.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-09
translation.text: Accumulated resources need an orderly manner of use. Lu follows Xiao Xu and brings the topic of appropriate conduct and social forms into the sequence.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-10
translation.text: Proper conduct can foster peaceful communication. Tai follows Lu as a condition of openness, ease, and stability after order has been established.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-11
translation.text: Nothing remains open and harmonious forever. Pi follows Tai to represent the possible reversal from communication into obstruction and estrangement.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-12
translation.text: Obstruction cannot last forever either. Tong Ren follows Pi, suggesting that renewed fellowship is one way relationships move beyond separation.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-13
translation.text: People who cooperate can attract further support and resources. Da You follows Tong Ren, representing a larger possession made possible by shared endeavor.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-14
translation.text: Great abundance brings the danger of overfilling and pride. Qian, humility, follows Da You as a necessary restraint when resources or power have expanded.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-15
translation.text: When abundance is joined to modesty, a community can become joyful and prepared. Yu therefore follows Qian in this sequence of social development.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-16
translation.text: Joy and readiness draw people into participation. Sui follows Yu and emphasizes following, responding, and moving together.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-17
translation.text: Following others in a cheerful spirit leads to obligations and work. Gu follows Sui and concerns the tasks of setting damaged affairs right.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-18
translation.text: After problems are confronted and repaired, greater responsibility becomes possible. Lin follows Gu and signifies approaching or overseeing what has grown.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-19
translation.text: An enterprise that has become substantial can be observed and assessed. Guan follows Lin, placing examination after the enlargement of affairs.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-20
translation.text: Observation makes discernment and connection possible. Shi He follows Guan, describing the act of biting through an obstruction so that separated parts can join.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-21
translation.text: Mere joining is not enough for lasting order; there must also be proper form. Bi, adornment, follows Shi He and concerns patterned expression.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-22
translation.text: Decoration can reach excess and exhaustion. Bo follows Bi and shows how outward forms may peel away when their basis is depleted.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-23
translation.text: Exhaustion is not the final state of things. Fu follows Bo because decline, once it reaches its limit, opens the possibility of return.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-24
translation.text: Returning to the proper course reduces reckless deviation. Wu Wang follows Fu, expressing an uncontrived or sincere manner of acting.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-25
translation.text: When conduct is free from reckless distortion, resources and virtue can be stored. Da Xu therefore follows Wu Wang as a form of substantial cultivation.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-26
translation.text: What has been stored can nourish life. Yi follows Da Xu and addresses both receiving sustenance and caring responsibly for others.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-27
translation.text: Nourishment makes action possible, but accumulated energy may exceed normal limits. Da Guo follows Yi to depict an extraordinary burden or imbalance.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-28
translation.text: An extreme condition cannot continue without exposing danger. Kan follows Da Guo and represents falling into difficulty or repeated pits.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-01-29
translation.text: A person in danger must find something to hold to. Li follows Kan and emphasizes attachment, support, and illumination as the upper canon closes.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-01
translation.text: The lower canon begins by tracing relations from Heaven and Earth to living things, then to men and women, spouses, generations, political ranks, and ritual order. The passage presents an ancient genealogy of social institutions through differentiation and relationship.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-02
translation.text: The relationship of spouses is expected to endure, so Heng follows Xian. Constancy becomes the principle that can sustain a bond beyond its first attraction.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-03
translation.text: No living thing can remain in one position forever. Dun follows Heng to mark the time when withdrawal becomes appropriate.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-04
translation.text: Withdrawal cannot be a permanent response to every situation. Da Zhuang follows Dun as strength returns and action becomes possible again.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-05
translation.text: Strength is not a final state; it can develop into forward movement. Jin follows Da Zhuang and expresses advancement.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-06
translation.text: Advancement can expose a person or a cause to injury. Ming Yi follows Jin, recalling the risk that light may be obscured when it moves forward.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-07
translation.text: Those wounded in the outside world return to their household for support. Jia Ren follows Ming Yi and turns attention from public adversity to family order.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-08
translation.text: Even a household's order can be exhausted and become divided. Kui follows Jia Ren as the condition of estrangement arising within established relations.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-09
translation.text: Estrangement creates practical obstacles. Jian follows Kui and depicts difficulty in finding a passable route.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-10
translation.text: Hardship cannot be the permanent destiny of a situation. Xie follows Jian and signifies the loosening of obstructions and release from difficulty.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-11
translation.text: Release and relaxation may also allow something to be lost. Sun follows Xie and represents reduction after a period of easing.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-12
translation.text: Reduction may create room for renewed increase. Yi follows Sun, setting gain and loss alongside each other as changing stages.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-13
translation.text: Increase that continues unchecked eventually demands a decision. Guai follows Yi and marks the point at which a firm resolution is required.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-14
translation.text: A decision changes relations and brings new encounters. Gou follows Guai, with meeting as its central idea.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-15
translation.text: Things that meet may then gather into a larger body. Cui follows Gou and symbolizes coming together.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-16
translation.text: Once a group is assembled, a new level of development can emerge. Sheng follows Cui and describes upward growth.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-17
translation.text: Rise without limit can lead to exhaustion or confinement. Kun follows Sheng, showing the cost of unrestrained ascent.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-18
translation.text: When pressure above becomes unbearable, one returns to the foundations below. Jing follows Kun and uses the well as an image of sustained communal support.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-19
translation.text: Even a well-established source of support requires renewal. Ge follows Jing and signifies reform or transformation.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-20
translation.text: After an old arrangement has been changed, a new one must be established. Ding follows Ge and evokes a ritual vessel used to nourish and order society.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-21
translation.text: The keeper of a significant vessel is represented by the eldest son. Zhen follows Ding and introduces movement, responsibility, and activation.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-22
translation.text: Movement cannot last without pauses. Gen follows Zhen as the principle of stopping at an appropriate time.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-23
translation.text: Stopping is not an end in itself. Jian, gradual progress, follows Gen when movement resumes in measured stages.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-24
translation.text: Progress calls for a destination or affiliation. Gui Mei follows Jian and uses marriage to depict an arrival into relationship.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-25
translation.text: Having found a place of belonging, things can flourish. Feng follows Gui Mei and denotes fullness or abundance.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-26
translation.text: Great fullness can become unstable, leaving people without their former place. Lu, the traveler, follows Feng.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-27
translation.text: A traveler may lack a secure place of welcome. Xun follows Lu and points toward entering, yielding, and finding a way through new surroundings.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-28
translation.text: Entry and communication can lead to pleasure. Dui follows Xun and expresses joy or agreeable exchange.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-29
translation.text: After a period of delight, things can disperse. Huan follows Dui and represents separation or the clearing away of congestion.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-30
translation.text: Dispersal cannot continue without limit. Jie follows Huan and introduces bounds, proportion, and restraint.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-31
translation.text: Appropriate limits create conditions for dependable trust. Zhong Fu follows Jie, emphasizing inward sincerity.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-32
translation.text: Trust should be brought into conduct. Xiao Guo follows Zhong Fu and depicts small departures or carefully limited action.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-33
translation.text: After moving beyond an obstacle, completion becomes possible. Ji Ji follows Xiao Guo as an image of affairs having been brought across.

translation.title: Sequence of the Hexagrams / XUGUA XUGUA-02-34
translation.text: No completion can close the process of change forever. Wei Ji follows Ji Ji, leaving the work unfinished and the possibility of a new beginning open.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-01
translation.text: Qian is associated with firmness, Kun with yielding; Bi suggests the pleasure of closeness, while Shi carries the anxiety of marshaling an army. The passage compares opposite qualities to sharpen the reader's sense of each hexagram.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-02
translation.text: Lin and Guan are set together through giving and seeking. One describes approaching or extending attention; the other describes observing and looking for understanding. Their contrast lies in the direction of engagement.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-03
translation.text: Zhun shows new life becoming visible without losing its ground, while Meng depicts an initially confused condition growing clearer. The pair contrasts emerging stability with the work of enlightenment.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-04
translation.text: Zhen begins or stirs movement; Gen brings movement to a stop. These paired trigrams display a basic rhythm of activation and restraint.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-05
translation.text: Sun and Yi are described as beginnings of decline and growth. Reducing and increasing are not isolated events but neighboring stages within larger cycles.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-06
translation.text: Da Xu is closely tied to the appropriate time for storing and restraining power; Wu Wang is linked here with unexpected misfortune. The pair warns against confusing readiness with immunity from events beyond control.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-07
translation.text: Cui means gathering, while Sheng concerns rising. Coming together and moving upward are related but distinct processes; an assembled group does not automatically produce advancement.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-08
translation.text: Qian, humility, makes a person light or unburdened, whereas Yu can drift toward ease and idleness. The comparison warns that pleasure without discipline may lose its constructive purpose.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-09
translation.text: Shi He is associated with biting or eating through an obstruction, while Bi is finally linked with the absence of excessive color. Effective connection and restrained ornament are compared.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-10
translation.text: Dui shows itself outwardly in delight and expression; Xun enters quietly and works beneath the surface. Visible joy contrasts with less obvious influence.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-11
translation.text: Sui involves following without clinging to former causes; Gu requires correcting and setting affairs in order. Adaptation and repair are different responses to changing circumstances.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-12
translation.text: Bo represents decay and peeling away; Fu represents return. One shows a process reaching its end, the other the beginning of recovery.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-13
translation.text: Jin is compared with the clarity of daytime, whereas Ming Yi describes brightness wounded or suppressed. Public visibility contrasts with an obscured light.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-14
translation.text: Jing is associated with a well's continuing access and supply, while Kun involves the meeting of difficulties and constraints. A reliable common resource contrasts with confinement.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-15
translation.text: Xian acts through immediate mutual response, whereas Heng is concerned with duration. Attraction and constancy are related, but a quick connection is not yet a lasting commitment.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-16
translation.text: Huan scatters or separates; Jie restrains and sets boundaries. A process of release is balanced by the need for proportion.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-17
translation.text: Xie eases pressure and loosens difficulty; Jian describes the difficulty that first blocks the path. The two hexagrams are opposite movements in a problem's course.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-18
translation.text: Kui refers to divergence toward the outside, while Jia Ren concerns the inner order of a household. Difference between groups is contrasted with order within a shared home.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-19
translation.text: Pi and Tai are contrasting kinds: obstruction and openness. The paired states show that communication and estrangement can exchange places.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-20
translation.text: Da Zhuang reminds a strong person to stop at the right point, while Dun counsels withdrawal when conditions are unsuitable. Strength is not always an instruction to advance.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-21
translation.text: Da You describes possession of much and the gathering of many supporters; Tong Ren describes affinity and cooperation. Material abundance and human fellowship are distinguished.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-22
translation.text: Ge removes the old, and Ding brings the new into use. Reform requires both taking away an exhausted arrangement and creating something that can replace it.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-23
translation.text: Xiao Guo concerns going somewhat beyond a normal limit; Zhong Fu is inward trustworthiness. A small exception in conduct is contrasted with a dependable moral center.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-24
translation.text: Feng entails many affairs and complications because fullness increases what must be managed. Lu depicts the traveler with few close companions and limited familiarity.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-25
translation.text: Li, like fire, moves upward; Kan, like water, moves downward. Their opposite directions provide a simple way of contrasting these two images.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-26
translation.text: Xiao Xu collects only limited resources, while Lu calls for active, careful movement rather than settling indefinitely. Accumulation and conduct are different needs.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-27
translation.text: Xu delays action while danger remains ahead; Song shows people drawn into disputes where closeness has broken down. Waiting and contention are distinct responses to difficulty.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-28
translation.text: Da Guo is an excessive burden that threatens overturning, while Gou signifies an encounter of yielding with firmness. Pressure and unexpected meeting are set side by side.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-29
translation.text: Jian uses the image of a woman waiting for marriage rites to unfold; Yi concerns nourishment in the proper way; Ji Ji signifies a settled completion. The text compresses three different dimensions of orderly development.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-30
translation.text: Gui Mei signifies a woman's marriage as the close of one social phase; Wei Ji presents a man's efforts reaching difficulty without final completion. These statements reflect the text's ancient role language and do not impose modern gender expectations.

translation.title: Miscellaneous Hexagrams / ZAGUA ZAGUA-01-31
translation.text: Guai means decisive resolution as strong lines overcome a yielding obstacle. The passage interprets this as the growth of the cultivated person's way and the decline of petty conduct.
